exp.0:3:
God tells Hosea to name his first child Jezreel. God announces that he will soon judge the house of Jehu and bring an end to the northern kingdom, called Israel.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Hosea, at a time when the people had turned away from God. Jezreel was the site of a massacre in the days of Jehu (2 Kings 9–10). Scholars explain in various ways why God judges it there: some think Jehu was too violent, and others that his family continued in idolatry. The child's name functions as a prophetic sign.

For today: God sees what we have done, even what seemed justified. Let us ask him to examine our hearts and guide us to obey him with humility.
exp.1:4:
Here it is said that the mother of these children was unfaithful and acted without shame. Here "played the harlot" means to be unfaithful, to prostitute oneself, and "lovers" are the men she goes after in place of her husband. She believes they give her everything she needs: food, water, clothing (wool and flax), oil and drink.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He compares Israel to an unfaithful wife who seeks other gods, such as Baal, and credits to them the blessings that really come from the Lord. That is why God announces a punishment, in the hope that she will recognize her error and return to Him, as the following verses say.

Today we can ask ourselves to whom we give thanks for what we have. It is easy to trust in work, money or success and forget that every good thing comes from God. Let us offer a sincere prayer of gratitude and place our trust in Him again.
exp.1:5:
God says that he is going to block the way of Israel, compared to an unfaithful wife. He will place thorns and a wall of brambles, so that she gets lost and cannot find her way.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. The people were following Baal, a Canaanite god, thinking that he gave them bread, wool, and oil. For this reason God blocks those paths. His purpose, according to the verses that follow, is that she will recognize who was truly sustaining her and will want to return to him.

For today: sometimes God allows obstacles to stop us when we go after things that take us away from him. If something blocks your way, do not harden your heart; ask yourself humbly what you are seeking and whether God is calling you to return to him.
exp.1:10:
God says he will bring an end to Israel's joy and all its religious celebrations: the yearly feasts, the new moons (the start of each month), and the sabbaths. The solemn feast days were their set holy occasions. Everything that seemed like life and blessing will come to a stop.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Hosea. He compares Israel to an unfaithful wife who goes after the Baals, Canaanite gods, and believes they give her the grain, the wine, and the wool. Because she forgot God, he takes away her blessings so that she will wake up. The feasts continued, but they were mixed with idolatry, so they did not please God. The punishment aims to bring her back to him.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our religion is sincere or just a custom. Let us thank God as the true giver of everything, and not trust in money, success, or pleasures. He corrects in order to restore us.
exp.1:11:
He says God will destroy Israel's vines and fig trees. She said these were her wages, the payment her lovers had given her. God will turn them into a thicket, a wild tangle of undergrowth, and the wild animals will eat what is left.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel is described as an unfaithful wife who credited her harvests to the Baal gods and not to the Lord. This judgment is a strong discipline. But the following context shows the goal: God will lead her into the wilderness and speak to her heart.

For today: ask yourself where you think what you have comes from. Thank God for your work, your food and your family, and do not put your security in things that can disappear. He corrects in order to restore.
exp.1:12:
It says God will call Israel to account for the days when she offered incense to the Baals, false gods of Canaan. Burning incense is what she did. The earrings and the jewels are what she wore as she dressed herself up for the festival, and she went after her lovers, that is, the idols, and forgot me. The saddest thing is that forgetting.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Hosea. He compares Israel to an unfaithful wife who credits her harvests to others and not to her husband. That is why judgment is coming. But the following verse shows the end of the punishment: God will lead her into the wilderness, speak to her heart, and give her hope.

For today: examine which things have taken the place of God in your heart, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Thank Him for what you have, and return to Him, who corrects in order to restore.
exp.1:13:
God says that, in spite of everything, he himself will draw his people back with tenderness. Here "allure" means to persuade, to draw someone gently and with affection. He will lead her into the wilderness, a place without distractions, and there he will speak to her tenderly, that is, with words of love and comfort.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel, compared to an unfaithful wife, went after the Baals, false gods, and credited its blessings to them. God announces judgment, but it does not end there: this verse is the turning point toward restoration. The wilderness recalls the time after Egypt, when the people came to know God up close.

For today: when you feel far from God or guilty, do not run from him. Set aside a while for silence, without noise or screens, and listen. He calls you not to condemn you, but to speak to you with love and restore you.
exp.1:19:
God says that he himself promises to marry his people again, and he will do it "in faithfulness," that is, with firm loyalty and commitment. The result is that they will "know the Lord." Here "know" does not mean only knowing facts, but having a close and personal relationship. To "betroth" means to make a commitment to marriage.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had been unfaithful to him, seeking other gods, and God had disciplined them. Even so, he promises to restore them. The verses before this one speak of peace, security, and a commitment forever, with justice, mercy, and tenderness.

For today: God does not give up on someone who walks away; his faithfulness is stronger than our failures. Today you can return to him with confidence and seek to know him better each day, speaking with him in prayer and reading his Word.
exp.2:3:
It says that Israel would spend a long time without its political and religious supports: without a king, without a prince, without a sacrifice, without an image (a pillar or sacred stone, which could be used in true or false worship), without an ephod (the priest's garment, linked to seeking God's guidance) and without teraphim (household idols). It is a time of emptiness and of being left without what was familiar.

God speaks through Hosea. The prophet bought his wife Gomer and kept her apart for a time in order to restore her. That illustrates how God deals with Israel, who had been unfaithful to him. Interpreters explain the "many days" in several ways, but the text that follows shows that the goal is the return to God.

For today: sometimes God allows you to lose things you trusted in, to teach you to seek Him alone. If you go through a time of emptiness, do not waste it: draw near to God with sincerity.
exp.3:8:
It says that the people and the priest will end up the same: both are guilty. God says he will punish their ways, that is, he will hold them accountable for how they live. The phrase about repaying them according to their deeds means that they will receive the consequences of what they did.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, in the northern kingdom of Israel. The priests were meant to teach God's law, but according to the chapter, they took advantage of the people's sin and did not guide them well. That is why the people and their leaders fall under the same judgment. Scholars agree that the sin belonged to the leaders as well as to the people.

For today: those who lead others, in the church or at home, carry a greater responsibility. And those who follow a leader cannot make excuses. Each person must seek God and live honestly before Him.
exp.3:15:
This verse says Israel has behaved like a stubborn young heifer that will not be led or accept the yoke. Then God asks a question with a tone of reproach: how can he now care for them as lambs in an open, quiet field? To shepherd means to tend a flock, and a wide, safe pasture is what is meant. The idea is that someone who rejects the shepherd cannot expect the peace of the meadow.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim. The people practiced idolatry and mixed their worship with pagan practices. God warns Judah not to follow that path and calls them not to go to Gilgal or Beth-aven, places of corrupted worship. Some understand the question as a warning of judgment; others, as a lament.

For today: we cannot ask for the protection of the Shepherd while we resist his guidance. Today you can hand over a specific area where you have been stubborn and ask him to teach you to obey.
exp.3:17:
Israel had gone to ruin: its drink had become sour (some understand this to refer to the feasting and drunkenness, since the Hebrew text is difficult), and it gave itself over to unfaithfulness persistently, that is, with stubbornness. Its rulers loved gifts, that is, bribes and presents, and this filled them with shame.

The prophet Hosea speaks, sent by God to the northern kingdom, also called Ephraim. The people worshiped idols and turned away from God like a stubborn heifer. The leaders, instead of caring for justice, sought their own gain.

Today this invites us to examine what we truly love. If money or comfort leads us to keep silent about the truth or to be unjust, we drift away from God. Ask Him for a faithful and honest heart, and act with integrity even when no one sees you.
exp.4:1:
It says that the people, in offering sacrifices, sank very deep into their sin. The Hebrew text is difficult, and some versions speak of slaughter or of deep rebellion. That is why God says that He will be the rebuker of them all: that is, the one who disciplines and punishes them.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He addresses the priests, the people, and the royal household in the northern kingdom. He accuses them of having been a snare and a net at Mizpah and Tabor, probably for leading others toward false worship, though it is not known with precision how.

For today: those who teach or lead others have a great responsibility. If you notice that you are drifting away from God, do not keep sinking: listen quickly to His correction, which seeks to bring you back to Him.
exp.4:4:
This verse says that Israel's pride is like a witness that accuses them and contradicts them before everyone. Their own arrogance will show that they are wrong. "Ephraim" is the name of the northern kingdom, and their stumbling means they will fall because of their sin. Even Judah, the southern kingdom, will fall along with them.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had turned away from Him and worshiped other gods; the Bible calls this unfaithfulness, like the betrayal in a broken marriage. God knows them well and warns them that their pride kept them from returning to Him.

For today: pride keeps us from recognizing our mistakes and returning to God. Ask Him today for humility to admit one specific fault, and take a step to correct it. He welcomes with grace whoever turns to Him with a sincere heart.
exp.4:5:
They will go with their flocks and their herds, meaning their sacrifices, to seek the Lord, but they will not find him. He has withdrawn himself from them.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel (also called Ephraim) and to Judah. The people had fallen into idolatry, which the text calls spiritual unfaithfulness, and their pride kept them from turning back to God. That is why, although they carried out religious offerings, their hearts remained far from him.

For today: performing rites, attending meetings, or giving offerings is not enough if the heart does not repent. God invites us to seek him with humility and sincerity, leaving behind whatever pulls us away from him. Today you can pray and ask him to show you what you need to change.
exp.4:9:
The leaders of Judah are said to have acted like those who move the boundary markers of a piece of land in order to take land that belongs to someone else. The stones that marked the limits of each property are the ones in view here. For this reason God announces that he will pour out his anger on them with force, as water is poured out.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. The people had turned away from him, and the northern kingdom (Ephraim) was in sin. Now Judah, the southern kingdom, is also accused of injustice and of breaking what God had established. The law forbade moving boundary markers (Deuteronomy 19:14). Interpreters differ on whether Hosea is speaking of literal theft of land or using the image to speak of crossing the limits of God's law in general.

Today, God sees how we use power. Ask yourself: is there some boundary of honesty that I am moving to my own advantage? Seek to live with justice and respect, even when no one sees you.
exp.4:11:
He says that God himself will be like a moth to Ephraim and like rottenness to Judah. A moth eats away at clothing, and rottenness decays wood, and both destroy slowly, without making any noise. Ephraim refers to the northern kingdom, Israel, and Judah to the southern kingdom.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. The leaders of Judah had moved the boundary stones, that is, they were violating what had been set in place, and Ephraim was following human commands and not the voice of God. For this reason God announces a judgment that wears away from within. Later, they will seek help from Assyria, but it will not be able to heal them.

For today: do not make light of small sins that are repeated, for they wear away life in silence. Return soon to God, who is the one who truly heals, and do not seek salvation in other sources.
exp.4:12:
This verse says that Ephraim (the northern kingdom, Israel) and Judah both came to see that they were sick and wounded because of their sin. But instead of seeking God, Ephraim went to Assyria and asked the king named Jareb for help. The name Jareb may be a personal name or a title, and its meaning is uncertain. That king could not heal them.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He is judging his people because they turned away from him and looked for security in alliances with foreign powers. God warns them that no human help could cure what only he can heal. But the passage ends with hope: God hopes they will acknowledge their sin and seek him.

For today: when you feel wounded, guilty, or afraid, do not run first to solutions that cannot heal the heart. Go to God first, with sincerity. He corrects, but he also restores.
exp.5:3:
God asks with sorrow: "What shall I do with you, Ephraim? What shall I do with you, Judah?" He tells them that their goodness, that is, their love and loyalty toward Him, lasts only as long as a morning cloud or the early dew, which the sun soon makes disappear. Ephraim was the common name for the northern kingdom, Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Just before this, the people had said beautiful words about returning to God and knowing Him. But God sees that their commitment is passing and shallow. That is why, in the verses that follow, He makes clear that what He desires most is mercy and the knowledge of Him, not only religious offerings.

For today: religious feelings that fade quickly are not enough. Ask God for a steady love and show it through small daily acts: praying, forgiving, helping, and obeying, even when you do not feel enthusiastic.
exp.5:5:
It tells us that God takes more pleasure in faithful, compassionate love (mercy) than in animal sacrifices. It also says he prefers that we truly know him, more than whole burnt offerings placed completely on the altar.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Ephraim and Judah claimed to love God, but their faithfulness lasted as briefly as the morning cloud or the dew, which soon vanish. They kept the rituals, but they broke the covenant, as the following verse shows.

Today we can examine whether our faith is only religious habit or whether it shows in how we treat others. This week, practice a specific act of mercy toward someone and seek to know God better through his Word.
exp.5:8:
It says that a group of priests acts like robbers who hide in ambush to attack someone. On the road they commit murder, and they do it by common agreement. The phrase about carrying out a horrible wickedness means that they carry out a terrible evil.

Some scholars believe this refers to real crimes committed near Shechem; others understand it in a more general way. It is not known with certainty.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He accuses Israel of breaking the covenant, and here he points to its religious leaders. Those who should have guided the people toward God were harming them. That is why the text goes on to speak of Israel's spiritual corruption.

For today: those who hold spiritual authority should care for others, not take advantage of them. We can pray for our leaders and examine how we ourselves use any influence we have.
exp.5:9:
God says he has seen something horrible among his people. The word "horrible" here means something frightening, a shameful condition. The phrase about spiritual unfaithfulness refers to Ephraim, who represents the northern kingdom, leaving God to follow other gods. The idea of being stained means that all of Israel was marked by that betrayal.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Just before this, he has mentioned crimes of violence, including by priests who were supposed to guide the people. God does not speak with indifference but like a husband wounded by unfaithfulness, an image Hosea uses throughout the book. His complaint is serious, but the book also shows his desire to restore his people.

For today: God sees what we sometimes hide. We can ask ourselves what things we have placed our trust or our heart in above him. With sincerity, let us return to him, who forgives and restores.
exp.6:0:
When God wanted to heal Israel, the wickedness of Ephraim came to light, and the evil of Samaria as well. "Ephraim" names the northern kingdom, and Samaria was its capital. "They practice deceit" means that they acted with lies and fraud. The text adds two images: a thief who breaks into houses, and a robber who plunders from outside.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, in the eighth century B.C., to a northern kingdom full of corruption, injustice and idolatry. When God tried to restore them, the people showed their true heart. Interpreters see the image of the thief and the robber as both internal disorder and external threat, and they do not always agree.

For today: when God confronts us, it is not to humiliate us but to heal us. If something hidden comes to light in your life, do not hide it or make excuses; bring it to God honestly and let Him heal it.
exp.6:2:
This verse says that the people of Israel, with their evil deeds and their lies, amuse and please their king and their rulers. Instead of being ashamed of sin, they celebrate it. The rulers are the leaders or authorities of the kingdom.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom (Israel, also called Ephraim, with its capital Samaria). God wanted to heal his people, but every time he drew near, more deceit and corruption appeared. The verses that follow show a court full of betrayal and drunkenness. Some scholars think it refers to political intrigues of that time, although the text does not give all the details.

For today: let us examine whom we try to please. It is easy to applaud lies or injustice in order to be liked or to gain advantages. Let us ask God for the courage to speak the truth with love, even when it costs us.
exp.6:3:
He says that the whole people is unfaithful to God, and that their desire to sin burns like a heated oven. The baker stops stoking the fire while the dough rises, but the embers keep burning. "Adulterers" speaks of physical unfaithfulness and also of leaving God for other gods.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel, in the north. He reminds them that he does not forget their wickedness. The leaders and the king rejoice in sin and in lies. Interpreters explain the image in different ways, but nearly all of them see a passion that does not go out and that waits for the moment to break out.

For today: do not believe that an evil desire goes away on its own just because it is quiet. Bring it to God in time, before it grows, and seek help in prayer and from trusted people.
exp.6:5:
This verse says that the hearts of Israel's leaders burned like an oven, full of crooked plans. The baker sleeps through the night while the oven still holds its coals, and in the morning the flame flares up again. In the same way, their evil plans seemed calm, but they stayed ready to catch fire.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Ephraim. He denounces the unfaithfulness and conspiracies of the court. The verses that follow say that several kings fell. Some think the image describes a palace plot, though the details are interpreted in different ways.

For today: anger, envy, or ambition that we keep quiet does not disappear; it only waits for a spark. Today we can bring those hidden desires before God, ask him for a clean heart, and seek peace before something catches fire.
exp.6:7:
It says that Ephraim, that is, the northern kingdom of Israel, mixed itself with the neighboring nations. It also compares him to a cake that was not turned over: one side was burned and the other side was raw, so it is no good to eat.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel was seeking alliances with other nations and copying their customs, instead of trusting the Lord. Meanwhile, the nation was growing weaker, and it did not even notice, as the verses that follow say.

For today: when we mix our faith with everything around us, we are left half-done, without maturing. We can ask God to show us where we are divided and to turn back to Him with our whole heart.
exp.6:15:
They turned back, the verse says, but not toward God Most High. They were like a deceitful bow, meaning a bent bow that misses its target even though it looks sound. Their leaders would fall by the sword for speaking with pride and arrogance. The verse says they would be mocked, and the people would laugh at them in Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, in the eighth century B.C., to the northern kingdom. God complains that they were seeking things like grain and new wine, not Him. Although He had strengthened them, they plotted evil. Some understand the reference to Egypt as the place they would go looking for help, or the place where they would be humiliated.

For today: changing direction or doing religious activities is not enough; one must turn to God Himself, with the heart. Examine whether you are seeking Him or only His blessings, and ask Him for sincerity.
exp.7:0:
It says that someone must put a trumpet to the mouth, that is, give a loud warning. An enemy will come swiftly like an eagle against the house of the Lord, because the people have broken the covenant, that is, they violated it, and rebelled against his law. The name of God appears here as the Lord.

Here God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel, the northern kingdom. The trumpet was an alarm signal before an attack. God warns of a coming judgment. Many understand that the "eagle" refers to an invader, probably Assyria, although the text does not name it here. "The house of the Lord" may refer to his people or to his land.

For today: it is not enough to say that we know God, as the text goes on to say, if we do not live in obedience. Today we can honestly examine where we have failed him, return to him, and obey him from the heart.
exp.7:5:
It says the calf of Samaria did not come from God, but from the hands of an Israelite craftsman. So it is not a god, only a manufactured object. "Craftsman" means a maker who works with his hands, and the calf is a young bull made as an idol. God announces that this idol will be broken to pieces.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom, Israel, whose capital was Samaria. The people had set up kings without consulting God and had made idols from their silver and gold. Scholars usually understand the calf as a cult idol in Samaria, although some debate the details of how it was used. God shows them the absurdity of worshiping something they made themselves.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we have made, such as money, success, or image, and to which we give the place of God. What we make cannot save us. Let us return to the true God, who truly sustains us.
exp.7:8:
Here the verse says that Israel, called Ephraim after its main tribe, went to seek help from Assyria. It is compared to a wild donkey, an untamed animal that roams on its own, stubborn and independent. The phrase "hired lovers" is an image: Ephraim paid gifts and tribute to foreign nations, like someone who pays for affection instead of trusting in their God. Assyria is the nation meant.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel sought political security through alliances instead of returning to the Lord. That is why God says they have sown the wind and will reap the whirlwind: their decisions would bring ruin. Scholars often connect this with the payments made to Assyria in the 8th century B.C.

For today: when we are afraid or in need, let us not run first to what seems safe, such as money, influence, or people. Let us first bring everything to God in prayer and ask for his guidance. He never leaves us alone.
exp.7:10:
It says that Ephraim, that is, the northern kingdom of Israel, filled the land with altars. They were supposed to serve for offering sacrifices and asking God for forgiveness, but they became a source of sin. It is as if God were saying: "So many altars, and all of them ended up being a place to sin."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel sought security in alliances with powers like Assyria, instead of trusting in God. It also practiced a religion full of rituals, but without obedience. That is why God rebukes them and announces that they will bear the consequences.

We can have a great deal of religious activity and still have our hearts far from God. Today it is good to ask ourselves whether our prayers, songs and service come from sincere obedience, or whether they are only a custom that calms the conscience. God seeks a faithful heart.
exp.7:11:
God says that he wrote to Israel the great and valuable things of his law, but the people treated them as if they were something strange, belonging to someone else, of no importance to them.

Here God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom, called Ephraim. The people filled the land with altars and sacrifices, yet they ignored what God had already taught them. Their religion was all outward appearance, without obedience. That is why God announces that he will remember their sin.

For today: it is not enough to have a Bible at home or to practice religious customs. Ask God to help you read his Word as something of your own, near and precious, and decide today to obey one specific thing it teaches you.
exp.8:3:
In exile, Israel will no longer be able to offer wine to God or sacrifices that please Him. Their bread will be like "bread of mourners", that is, the bread of people who are grieving a death, which according to the law made anyone who ate it unclean. That bread would only serve to satisfy hunger, not to be taken to the house of the Lord.

The prophet Hosea speaks, sent by God to Israel (called Ephraim) in the eighth century B.C. There was idolatry and unfaithfulness, and God warns that they will lose the land and live among foreign peoples. The exact details of that exile are understood in several ways, but the central message is clear.

For today: worship is not a simple ritual. If my heart is far from God, my offerings and my songs lose their meaning. Today I can draw near to Him sincerely, acknowledging my failures and returning to Him with humility.
exp.8:4:
This verse is a question that God asks through the prophet. It asks what the Israelites will do when their sacred festivals come, the solemn day and the feast of the Lord. The question suggests that they will not be able to celebrate them as they did before.

Hosea speaks to Ephraim, the name given to the northern kingdom, Israel. Because of their unfaithfulness and their idolatry, the prophet announces that they will be carried into exile, to Assyria and Egypt. There they will not have the temple and will not be able to offer sacrifices, and their food would be unclean according to the law.

For today: let us not take worship and spiritual privileges for granted. If our hearts turn away from God, religious practices become empty. Let us seek a sincere relationship with Him, not merely carry out rituals.
exp.8:5:
It says that the people of Israel go into exile because of the destruction that is coming. Egypt will gather them, that is, it will be their refuge or their place of captivity, and Memphis, an Egyptian city famous for its tombs, will bury them. What they valued most, the treasures they had silver for, will be overrun by thorns, and nettles will grow in their abandoned houses.

The prophet Hosea speaks, sent by God to Israel (also called Ephraim). He warns that their idolatry and injustice will bring judgment. Their feasts and sacrifices do not please God because their hearts are far from Him. Many understand that Egypt here is a symbol of returning to slavery, though some take it literally.

For today: let us not confuse religion with a sincere relationship with God. Let us examine whether what we care for most, such as money and possessions, occupies the place that only God deserves. Let us return to Him with our whole heart, before what we love is left empty.
exp.8:7:
It says that Ephraim, that is the northern kingdom of Israel, was supposed to be like a watchman standing guard for his God. But the prophet whom God sends finds traps on every road he travels, and hostility even inside the house of God. A watchtower is a tower or lookout post.

The prophet Hosea speaks, roughly 750 to 725 years before Christ, when Israel had sunk into idolatry and injustice. Some understand that Ephraim was meant to keep watch together with the prophet; others, that Ephraim spied on the prophet with bad intent. In both cases, the people rejected the voice of God.

Today, ask yourself whether you listen with humility to someone who corrects you with truth, or whether you treat them as an enemy. A biblical and loving correction can be a gift from God.
exp.8:10:
This verse says that Ephraim's glory, that is, its greatness and blessing, will fly away like a bird. And the loss will not come slowly: it will reach from birth, from the womb, and from conception. In other words, the children, who were a sign of prosperity, will stop being born or will not grow up.

The prophet Hosea speaks on God's behalf to the northern kingdom, called Ephraim. The people had fallen into the idolatry of Baal-peor and had become corrupt. God recalls that at the beginning he saw them as fresh grapes in the desert, but now judgment is coming. Many understand the loss of children to be a direct punishment for their sin.

For today: whatever we value most, whether family, success, or recognition, cannot take the place of God. If we let it, it becomes fragile. Let us put God first and receive his blessings with gratitude.
exp.8:12:
Hosea says that he saw Ephraim, that is, the northern kingdom of Israel, likened to the city of Tyre: established in a beautiful and secure place. But that well-being will not last, because Ephraim will have to hand over its children to the enemy who kills. Some words in the Hebrew are difficult, and the translations vary a little.

The prophet Hosea speaks, bringing God's message. Israel was prosperous, but it had filled itself with idolatry and disloyalty. For this reason God announces judgment: the peace they saw would not protect them from the consequences of turning away from Him.

For today: comfort and success are not proof that everything is right with God. Ask yourself honestly in what you trust most: in what you have, or in the Lord. Return to Him while there is still time.
exp.8:15:
Hosea says that Ephraim, that is, the northern kingdom of Israel, has been struck like a tree that is wounded. Its root has dried up, and it will no longer bear fruit. The root is the base of the plant that holds it up and feeds it. Even if they have children, God will take the life of the beloved children of their womb.

The prophet Hosea speaks here, announcing God's judgment. The people had abandoned God through idolatry and injustice, and Gilgal is mentioned as a place of their wickedness. Some think the sentence before this is from the prophet, and others think it expresses the voice of God; the text does not fully make this clear. The punishment is harsh, but it aims to show how serious it is to ignore God.

For today: let us not allow religious habit to harden our hearts. If God corrects us through his Word, let us listen quickly and return to him, because a life without obedience ends up dry, even when it looks strong on the outside.
exp.9:12:
It says that Israel sowed wickedness and therefore reaps deception. The images of the field show that what a person plants is what they harvest. Plowing wickedness and reaping iniquity are farming images. The fruit of lies is a harvest that promises much and gives nothing. The people trusted in their own way and in their many mighty men, not in God.

The passage presents God speaking through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Ephraim or Israel. Earlier, God had invited them to sow righteousness and to seek the Lord. But they preferred injustice, idols, and military strength. For this reason the following text announces the destruction of their fortresses.

For today: examine where your security rests. Every decision is a seed. If you trust only in your money, your strength, or your plans, the harvest will disappoint. Sow justice and mercy, and seek God first.
exp.10:0:
God loved Israel from its beginnings, when it was like a child, and he brought it out of Egypt, calling it "my son." The word translated as "child" speaks of the people's youth, that is, of its beginning as a nation.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He reminds the Israelites of the northern kingdom, also called Ephraim, how much he cared for them during the exodus. Even so, they turned away and served the Baals, false gods. The verses that follow show God as a father who teaches his son to walk. In Matthew 2:15, the New Testament quotes this phrase when speaking of Jesus; many see it as a connection between Israel and Christ.

God loved us first, before we responded to him. Today you can remember how he has cared for you, even when you sometimes did not notice it, and return to him with gratitude and trust.
exp.10:1:
This verse says that, while God was calling Israel, the people kept moving away from Him. Instead of answering Him, they sacrificed to the Baals, which were false gods of Canaan, and burned incense to carved images, that is, to the sculpted idols.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, in the eighth century BC, to the northern kingdom (Israel, also called Ephraim). First He recalls His love as a father: He brought Israel out of Egypt and cared for it like a small child. That is why the pain is greater: the people forgot who had cared for them and went after other gods.

Today we can ask ourselves what things take the place that belongs to God: money, success, comfort. When He calls us, we sometimes pretend not to hear. Remembering how much He has cared for us helps us return and answer Him with trust and gratitude.
exp.10:3:
God says he led Israel with human cords, that is, with gentle and close care, with cords of love. He is compared to someone who loosens the yoke from the animal's jaw so that it can eat with more ease, and then brings the food close to it.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He remembers how he cared for Israel, here called Ephraim, like a little child he taught to walk. Yet the people turned away and worshiped the Baals. For this reason the warning of judgment follows. Some understand the loosened yoke as an image of freedom; the general meaning is God's tender care.

For today: think of some help you have received that you did not recognize as God's care. Thank him today and respond with trusting obedience, without hardening your heart.
exp.10:4:
This verse says that the people of Israel (called here Ephraim) would not return to Egypt, but that Assyria, another foreign power, would be their king. The reason is clear: they refused to change course, that is, they refused to turn back to God.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Hosea. Before this, God recalls how he cared for Israel like a father who teaches his child to walk, leading them with bands of love. Even so, the people did not recognize his care. Many understand that Egypt represents a return to slavery, and that Assyria was the empire that ended up dominating them. God speaks with pain, not with coldness.

For today: when God corrects us, it is not to destroy us, but to call us back to himself. Today we can ask ourselves: in what area am I ignoring his care? Answering with humility keeps other things from ending up ruling our lives.
exp.10:5:
This verse says the war will reach the cities of Israel and destroy their towns and villages. It means that the coming conflict will bring total destruction to their settlements. The sword will fall on their cities, and their branches will be consumed. Some scholars also understand that it may allude to their false leaders or to their political alliances.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim. God had shown them love like a careful father, but they did not want to return to him. For this reason judgment would come, and Assyria would be the power that would dominate them. Even so, the verses that follow show God's pain at having to correct them.

For today: when we trust only in our own plans and reject God's guidance, we suffer the consequences. Today you can ask him for wisdom before you decide, remembering that his correction comes from a love that does not give up.
exp.10:6:
This verse says that God's people are stuck to their rebellion, like someone who will not let go. Even though they are called toward the Most High, that is, toward God, no one is willing to lift him up or honor him. The verse's comment on the word for "bent" is that it means clinging or holding fast, and its comment on the word for "exalt" is that it means praising and placing God in the highest place.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel, also called Ephraim. First he recalls his fatherly love, but the people rejected him, and so he announces the consequences under Assyria. Yet soon his heart is moved, and he decides not to destroy them completely.

Today we can ask ourselves whether there is something we are holding on to even though God calls us to let it go. Responding quickly to his voice, with humility and praise, opens the door to his mercy, which keeps seeking us.
exp.10:9:
It says that one day the people of Israel will follow the Lord. God himself will roar like a lion, and not as a threat against them but as a strong call. When they hear his voice, his children will come trembling, that is, astonished, moved, and hurrying, from the west, which in the text may refer to the lands of the sea or distant lands.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He has just said that his heart is stirred and that he will not completely destroy Ephraim, because he is God and not a man. Although Israel deserved judgment, God promises to bring them back. The roar of a lion is sometimes used for judgment, but here it seems to be a call that gathers.

For today: when you have drifted away from God, do not doubt his mercy. His voice may sound firm, but it seeks to bring you home. Respond quickly, with humility, and walk after him again.
exp.11:3:
This verse says that Jacob, while still in his mother's womb, grabbed his brother Esau by the heel. It also says that, as an adult, through his strength he wrestled with an angel and prevailed.

The prophet Hosea speaks, sent by God to the northern kingdom, called Ephraim. The people sought safety in alliances with Assyria and Egypt, and not in God. Hosea reminds them of the story of their ancestor Jacob: a cunning man who, in the end, wept and begged God for mercy. Some think this is a call to repentance; others think it also points out Jacob's faults.

When you feel weak or afraid, do not trust your own plans. Cling to God in prayer, even with tears, and wait for his blessing.
exp.11:5:
This verse says that the Lord, to whom Israel must return, is the God of hosts, that is, the God of all power, and that his name is to be remembered. The name by which God wishes to be remembered and called upon is the name the verse is about. The name is written in an old form that the reader may recognize from older Bibles, but its meaning is the name of God itself.

Hosea speaks in God's name to the people of the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim. He reminds them of the story of Jacob, who wrestled with the angel and sought God's blessing at Bethel. Some understand that Hosea presents Jacob as an example of seeking God; others also see a warning in his deceitful character. Then he calls them to return to God.

For today: remember who God is, powerful and faithful, and return to him with humility. Practice justice and mercy in your work and in your dealings with others.
exp.11:6:
The verse you are reading is Hosea 12:7, which says: "A merchant loves to defraud with dishonest scales in his hands."

The verse calls on the reader to return to their God. The word for this means to turn back, to change direction. It also calls for practicing mercy, which means steadfast love and kindness, and justice, which means doing what is right. And it calls the reader to wait on God continually, that is, to trust in Him patiently and without growing weary.

The prophet Hosea speaks to the people of the northern kingdom, called Ephraim or Israel. He reminds them of their ancestor Jacob, who wrestled, wept, and sought God at Bethel. Then he rebukes them, because they used false scales, cheated others, and considered themselves innocent because they were rich. God offers them the chance to return.

Today, true faith shows in daily dealings. Examine your work and your business: be honest, just, and compassionate, and trust in God more than in your money.
exp.11:7:
This verse says that Ephraim (the northern kingdom, Israel) is like a dishonest merchant. In his hand he holds false scales, that is, weights tampered with to cheat the customer. He also loves to oppress, which means he enjoys abusing and taking advantage of others. Some understand that God compares him to the traders of Canaan.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He has just called the people to return to Him and to practice mercy and justice. But Ephraim boasts of his wealth and says that no one will find sin in him. God shows him that his prosperity is stained by fraud.

Today, we can examine our own scales: are we honest at work, in our prices, in our accounts and in our payments? Making money is not wrong, but God calls us to do it with truth and to treat others well.
exp.11:9:
It says that God is still the same God of Israel who brought them out of Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Ephraim, that is, the northern kingdom, considered itself rich and innocent, although it used false weights and oppressed others. Scholars interpret this in two ways: as a warning of losing everything and returning to a simple life, or as a promise of restoration. Both ideas fit the passage.

For today: do not trust in your riches or in your own righteousness. Remember that everything you have comes from God, and live with honesty, humility, and gratitude.
exp.11:12:
Here Jacob, the ancestor of Israel, had to flee to the land of Aram, which was the region of Syria and Mesopotamia. There he worked for another man in exchange for a wife, and for her he tended sheep.

Here God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim, which had turned away from Him. He reminds them of their humble origin: their father Jacob was a fugitive and a servant. Then the text contrasts this with what God did afterward: He brought Israel out of Egypt through a prophet, Moses, and cared for them. Interpreters disagree about the exact tone, but the contrast seems clear: Israel was to remember its smallness and the faithfulness of God.

For today: remembering where God brought us from helps us live with gratitude rather than pride. Today you can thank Him for a difficult season in which He sustained you.
exp.11:13:
God says that he brought Israel out of Egypt through a prophet, Moses, and through a prophet he cared for them. But Ephraim, who stands for the northern kingdom, angered him bitterly, that is, with sins that deeply offend him. Because of this, the guilt for their killings and violence will fall upon him, and his Lord will return his shame to him, that is, the contempt and mockery he showed toward God.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, who calls Israel to repentance. Earlier he recalled how Jacob was humble and worked as a shepherd. Now he sets that past against the idolatry and injustice of the people. God reminds them that he always guided them with care, but they repaid him badly.

For today: God has cared for us more than we notice. Before we harden our hearts, let us remember his goodness and respond with gratitude and obedience, not with pride.
exp.12:2:
It says that Israel, because it has abandoned God, will soon disappear. It uses four images of things that pass away: the morning mist, the early dew that the sun dries up, the chaff that the wind carries off when grain is threshed, and the smoke that rises out of the smokehouse opening. The smoke image is explained as referring to an opening or window through which smoke goes out.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Ephraim, the most important tribe of the northern kingdom, had been respected, but it fell into the worship of Baal. Now they were making silver idols and even kissing calves. God warns that what seemed strong will have no future without Him. Right after, He reminds them that only He saved them from Egypt.

For today: everything we put in place of God, such as money, fame, or security, fades away like smoke. Today you can ask yourself what you are resting your life on, and trust God again, the only One who endures.
exp.12:4:
God tells his people that he "knew" them while they were in the wilderness, in a dry land with no resources. Here "knew" means to care for, accompany, and love closely, not merely to know who they were. It was God who sustained them when there was no water and no food.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, Israel (also called Ephraim). He reminds them of the time after leaving Egypt, when they depended completely on him. He does this because, once they were prosperous, they became filled with pride and forgot God, as the following verse says. For this reason the people are warned of judgment.

For today: Remember the dry seasons when God sustained you. Remembering it helps you stay thankful and humble when things go well, and not forget where your help comes from.
exp.12:9:
God asks Israel where the king is in whom it trusted. He asks them to look and see whether that king, with his judges and princes, can deliver the people and their cities. The question is ironic: there is no one who can save them.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim. The people had asked for a king so that they could be like the other nations, and they leaned on human leaders more than on God. Now judgment is coming, but the verse before says that their help is in God. Scholars debate exactly which king or moment is in view, but the general meaning is clear.

For today: examine where you place your ultimate trust, whether in a leader, a government, money, or your own plan. Those things may help, but they cannot save you. Turn your confidence back to God, who still offers help.
exp.12:12:
It says that pains like those of a woman giving birth will come upon Ephraim. But the problem is that he is a son without wisdom: instead of coming out at the right time, he stays stuck at the moment of birth, at the point where he should be born. The word "unwise" here refers to a foolish person who does not understand what he should do.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Ephraim. He rebukes them for their sin and their stubbornness, since they did not repent in time. The image of birth shows that there was a chance to move forward, but they resisted. Some scholars see judgment here; others also see a call to return.

Today, we should not delay repentance. If God shows us a mistake, it is wise to respond quickly and with humility, because he wants to give us new life and not leave us stuck.
exp.12:14:
It says that Ephraim, the northern kingdom of Israel, seems to be prospering among its brothers, the other tribes. But God will send an east wind, a dry and scorching wind that comes from the desert. That wind will dry up its springs and its wells. Then an enemy will plunder the treasure, that is, all the valuable objects of the land. The words for spring and fountain both refer to a source of water.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had turned away from Him through idolatry and political alliances. Most readers understand the wind to represent the invasion of Assyria, although the text presents it as both a real wind and a symbol. The following verse announces the fall of Samaria, its capital.

For today: prosperity is not proof that all is well with God. Examine your heart, and do not trust in your achievements, but in the Lord, who is the fountain that never runs dry.
exp.13:4:
God promises that He Himself will be like the dew to Israel. In dry lands, dew refreshes and gives life during the night. Thanks to that care, the people will blossom like a lily and spread their roots like the cedars of Lebanon, that is, they will grow with strength and stability.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had turned away from Him to trust in Assyria, in war horses, and in idols. But now the people repent, and God responds with forgiveness and healing: He says He will heal their rebellion and love them freely.

When we return to God, He not only forgives but also renews and strengthens us. We can stop looking for security in things that fail and receive from Him new life and deep roots.
exp.13:5:
It says that the restored people will grow like a healthy tree. Its branches will spread out. Its beauty will be like that of the olive tree, an evergreen and valuable tree, and its fragrance will be pleasant like the cedars and forests of Lebanon, famous for their scent.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had turned away from God through idols and rebellion, but now God promises to heal them and love them wholeheartedly, because his anger has passed. This is a promise of restoration for whoever returns to him.

For today: if you feel far from God or damaged by your mistakes, you can return to him with confidence. He forgives and also makes a new life grow. That growth is usually gradual, like that of a tree, so stay close to God each day.
exp.8:6:
The verse says that the time of punishment has come, the time of payback has arrived, and Israel is going to know it. "Punishment" here means a moment when God steps in to judge, and "retribution" means receiving what has been deserved. The prophet is called a fool and the inspired man is called insane, because of the greatness of the people's wickedness and their deep hostility.

Hosea, a prophet of God, speaks to the kingdom of Israel (Ephraim), which lived in idolatry and injustice. Scholars debate whether the insults are spoken by the people mocking the prophet, or whether Hosea quotes them with irony. Either way, the people rejected the warning, and the exile was drawing near.

For today: when someone corrects us with truth, let us not dismiss it with mockery or anger. Better to ask humbly whether God is speaking to us, and to change in time.
exp.6:14:
God says that He trained Israel, preparing them for their task, and that He strengthened their arms, meaning He gave them power and victory. Even so, they plot evil against Him: they planned wrongdoing and turned away from their God.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, in the northern kingdom (Israel, also called Ephraim). He complains like a wounded father: He had rescued and strengthened them, yet they sought help from other nations and cried out only for grain and wine, not for Him.

For today: let us recognize that all strength, health, and ability come from God. Instead of using His gifts to live far from Him, let us give Him thanks today and seek Him sincerely, not only when we need something.
exp.3:4:
In this verse, God says that his judgment will reach everyone: you will stumble by day, the prophet will stumble with you by night, and your mother, who stands for the nation, will be destroyed. "Destroy" means to wipe out completely, the way a tree is cut down at the root. "Stumble" points to ruin, not just a small misstep.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the priest and the people of northern Israel. There was lying, violence and idolatry, and the leaders were not teaching the law. Some think that "day" and "night" show that no one will escape; others think the fall will be total. The text does not fully settle this.

For today: Those who teach or guide others carry a great responsibility before God. And each of us can ask whether we are truly seeking his Word, because without it we lose our way.
exp.4:8:
Ephraim, which represents the northern kingdom of Israel, will be laid waste on the day God brings judgment upon it. The phrase "laid waste" means left in ruins. God adds that this is not a surprise to Him or to His people: among the tribes of Israel He had already proclaimed what is certain, a true and firm warning.

Here God speaks through the prophet Hosea. The people had been unfaithful to Him, worshiping idols and forgetting their covenant with Him. That is why the punishment was not arbitrary: they already knew what God expected and what would happen if they abandoned Him.

For today: God speaks to us clearly in His Word because He loves us. When we feel His correction, we can see it as an invitation to return to Him before the consequences grow.
exp.0:4:
It says that God himself will break the military power of Israel, the northern kingdom. The bow was the main weapon of war, so it stands for their strength and their security. "On that day" points to a moment of judgment that was drawing near. The place is the Valley of Jezreel, a plain where many battles were fought.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He asks him to give his son the name Jezreel, a name carrying a warning. Jezreel recalled the blood shed in the time of Jehu, and God announces that he will call them to account. Israel trusted in its army and its alliances, not in God. Scholars debate exactly which events the "blood of Jezreel" refers to, but the central message is clear: judgment will come.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether money, work or plans. All of that can fail, but God does not.
exp.8:2:
This verse says that the people of Israel, here called Ephraim, will lose their place in the land of the LORD. They will go back to Egypt, and in Assyria they will eat food that is unclean, that is, impure according to the law of Moses. "Unclean food" refers to what the law forbade Israel to eat, and "Ephraim" is the main tribe of the northern kingdom.

The one speaking is the prophet Hosea, announcing God's message. Israel had turned away from God to worship idols and to trust in its harvests and its profits. Hosea warns that there will be consequences, and exile is the most serious of them. Some understand "return to Egypt" literally, and others understand it as an image of returning to slavery.

For today: check where you place your deepest trust, whether in God or in your income and achievements. God calls us to return to Him with sincerity, before other things pull us away from His presence.
exp.5:1:
He says that God, who wounded his people, will also heal them. The verse says he will revive us, a plain phrase that needs no explanation. The expression about a brief span of time, "after two days... on the third day," indicates a short interval before God raises them up. They hope to live in his presence.

The speakers are the Israelites who say, "Come, let us return to the LORD." However, the next verse shows that God regards their love as fragile, like the morning cloud or the dew that soon disappears. Some understand this as a shallow repentance; others, as a sincere hope. Christians often see here a shadow of the resurrection of Christ, although the text does not say so directly.

Today, we can trust that God restores. But our turning back to him should be constant, not just a passing impulse.
exp.4:13:
God says here that he will be like a lion to Ephraim (the northern kingdom, Israel) and like a young lion to Judah (the southern kingdom). The words "tear them to pieces" describe him attacking and carrying off his prey, the words "then go away" describe him leaving afterward, and the words "carry them off where no one can rescue them" mean that no one will be able to save them from his hand.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. The two kingdoms had turned away from God and sought help from Assyria and its king, instead of seeking him. Because of this, God allows judgment. The verses that follow show that he withdraws so that they will recognize their sin and seek him. Some understand this as the Assyrian invasions; the text gives no further detail.

For today: when things become difficult, do not run first to human solutions. If God corrects you, remember that his aim is to bring you back to himself, and you can return to him today with sincerity.
exp.4:10:
Ephraim, who is the northern kingdom of Israel, is oppressed and crushed under God's judgment. "Oppressed" means mistreated or weighed down. "Determined to follow" means to be set on going after something, committed to it. The reason is that Ephraim chose to follow worthless idols.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He had given his truth to the people, but they preferred other gods. The idols were empty and could not save anyone, so following them led straight to ruin. That is why God announces punishment, and later shows that seeking help from Assyria would not heal them.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we are following. Before following trends, pressures, or traditions, it is wise to compare them with the Word of God and ask him for wisdom to choose his way.
exp.10:8:
God says he will not unleash the full force of his anger on Ephraim, another name for the northern kingdom of Israel, and he will not destroy it again. He gives the reason: "For I am God and not man." He is the Holy One, present among his people, and he does not respond the way a person does when wronged. The closing line, "I will not come in wrath," can be taken in more than one way: that he will not come as an enemy bent on destruction, or that he will not come in human anger.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. His people had rebelled and turned away from him, and yet God shows a heart torn between judgment and compassion. He recalls Admah and Zeboiim, cities that were destroyed, but he says he will not do the same to Israel.

For today: when you fail, do not think that God reacts like a wounded and vengeful person. His holiness includes mercy. Return to him with confidence and let his patience move you to change.
exp.1:3:
It says that God will have no compassion on this woman's children, because they were born in the midst of a life of adultery. "Adultery" is the meaning here, and "compassion" means mercy or forgiveness.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. The mother represents Israel, the people who had been unfaithful to him by worshiping idols and trusting in other lovers. The children are the people of that generation, who followed the same path. Many understand this as a severe judgment, but the book goes on to promise restoration: God disciplines to call his people back.

For today: examine the things in which you place your trust in place of God, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Return to him sincerely, for his warnings aim to heal us, not destroy us.
exp.1:6:
It says that Israel, portrayed as an unfaithful wife, will pursue her lovers (the idols and the allied nations), but she will not be able to catch them or find them. Then she will say: "I will return to my first husband, for then I was better off than now."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. His people had left him to worship Baal, believing that the idols gave them bread, wool and oil. God blocks their paths with thorns, not only to punish, but so that she will recognize where all good things come from. Many see here a first step toward repentance, although her motive still seems self-interested.

Today we might ask ourselves: in what things do I seek security apart from God? When those things fail, it is not the end, but an invitation to return to Him, who always welcomes the one who comes back.
exp.1:18:
God promises to take his people as his bride forever. "Betroth" means to bind oneself to someone in marriage. He will do this "in righteousness and justice," meaning in what is right and fair, and "in loving devotion and compassion," a love that is faithful and moved with tender feeling.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to Israel, which had been unfaithful to him by worshiping the Baals, false gods. Before this verse, God promises to remove those false names and to give peace. Hosea himself lived through a painful marriage, which serves as an image of God's faithful love toward a people who had turned away.

For today: if you have failed or feel far from God, he does not offer you a passing relationship or one based on your merits. You can return to him with confidence, receive his forgiveness, and let his love guide your decisions and how you treat others.
exp.0:1:
It says God began to speak through Hosea and told him to marry a prostitute and have children with her. The phrase "prostitute" and "children of adultery" here also serve as an image of spiritual unfaithfulness: turning away from God to follow other gods.

The LORD speaks, and the message is addressed to the kingdom of Israel, which had filled itself with idolatry. God uses Hosea's life as a visible sign: just as that woman would be unfaithful to her husband, the people had been unfaithful to God. Scholars disagree about whether the scene was literal or symbolic, and about whether Gomer was already unfaithful before the marriage or became so afterward.

For today: God calls us to a loyalty of the heart, not merely to keeping up religion. Ask yourself what things occupy the place that belongs to God, and return to Him with confidence.
exp.7:3:
It says that the people of Israel set up kings and rulers without consulting God or seeking his approval. Moreover, they made idols out of their silver and gold, and this would lead them to their own destruction. The verse says "princes" are rulers, and that their idols were made of silver and gold, bringing about their own destruction.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom, Israel. They claimed to know him, yet they lived apart from him. That is why God shows them that their politics and their religion did not come from obedience. Scholars debate exactly which kings are meant, but the central idea is clear: they acted on their own.

For today: before making important decisions, such as work, family, or money, ask God and seek his guidance in the Bible. It is also wise to examine where we place our resources, so that they do not become idols that end up harming us.
exp.2:2:
Then Hosea tells the woman he has taken back: "You must live with me for many days. You must not be promiscuous or belong to another, and I will do the same for you." The words "promiscuous" and "belong to another" describe a life of unfaithfulness, the kind of life she had been living.

The promise "I will do the same for you" means that Hosea will also remain faithful to her, staying loyal in the same way he asks her to.

Hosea speaks at God's command. His marriage to an unfaithful woman is a picture of God's love for Israel, which had turned after other gods. The verse that follows applies this: Israel would spend many days without king or worship, in a time of waiting and correction, before returning to seek God.

For today: God's love does not give up, but it also knows how to set limits in order to heal. If something has taken the place of God in your heart, He invites you to a time of stillness, to letting it go, and to returning to Him with trust.
exp.13:2:
Assyria will not save us, and we will not put our trust in horses, which stood for military strength. We will never again call the work of our own hands our gods. In you, the fatherless, the one who has no one to turn to, finds compassion.

Hosea speaks to Israel, which had looked for help in alliances with other nations and in idols. God invites them to return to him, and even gives them the words they can say. In the verse that follows, God answers by promising to heal their rebellion and to love them freely.

For today: consider what you are placing your security in, such as money, influence, or your own plans. Give these to God sincerely, and come to him as you are, with your emptiness and needs, trusting that he will receive you with mercy.
exp.1:8:
God says that he is going to take back what he had given: the grain and the new wine when their time comes, and also the wool and linen that were given to cover her nakedness. "Take back" means he will remove them; the "time" is the proper moment, the ripeness; "nakedness" is the shame of her poverty.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to Israel, pictured as an unfaithful wife. She credited her blessings to Baal and to her lovers, without recognizing that they came from God. That is why he takes away his gifts, not as simple punishment, but so that she will wake up and return to him, her first husband.

For today: let us remember that everything good we have comes from God. Let us give thanks today instead of trusting in money, success, or things that cannot sustain us, and return to him with sincerity.
exp.13:8:
Whoever is wise, let him understand these things; whoever is discerning, let him know them. The ways of the LORD are right, and the righteous walk in them, but the rebellious stumble in them. This is the meaning: the one who is wise and discerning must grasp what God has said throughout this whole book. The ways of the LORD are right, meaning upright and just. Those who obey, the righteous, will walk securely along them. The rebellious, those who oppose God, will stumble and fall on those very same paths.

Hosea closes his book with this reflective statement. Throughout the book, God accused Israel (Ephraim) of idolatry and unfaithfulness, but He also called them to return to Him. Just before, God promises to heal and renew those who repent. This verse is the final invitation to think carefully and choose well.

For today: wisdom is not merely knowing things, but obeying God. Think of one area of your life where you have resisted His guidance, and surrender it to Him today with trust, believing that His way is good.
exp.1:9:
God says that now he is going to expose Israel's "folly," meaning her shameful and senseless conduct, in the sight of her "lovers," the false gods and the nations she trusted in. No one will be able to rescue her from his hands. The word "rescue" means to save or set free.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel, which is compared to an unfaithful wife. She credited her harvests and wealth to Baal, a Canaanite god, without recognizing that everything came from the Lord. For this reason God announces judgment. Many understand that his goal is to correct her and bring her back to himself, as is seen later in the book.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we are putting in God's place: money, success, or comfort. Let us give thanks to him for what we have, because every good gift comes from his hands.
exp.1:17:
God promises to make a covenant for his people with the beasts of the field, the birds of the air, and the creatures that crawl on the ground, so that these creatures will no longer pose a threat to them. He also says he will abolish the bow, the sword, and battle from the land. In this way, his people will be able to rest peacefully and without fear. The phrase "make them lie down in safety" means that they will rest with confidence.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to Israel, which had been unfaithful to him by worshiping the Baals. Even so, God promises to restore the relationship, like a husband who forgives. Many understand this peace as an image of complete reconciliation, but interpreters explain it in different ways, depending on whether they see it as pointing to the future or to a spiritual fulfillment.

For today: when fear or insecurity keeps you from resting, remember that God is the one who gives true peace. Speak to him honestly, entrust your fears to him, and seek to live close to him, who promises to restore what is broken.
exp.13:7:
Ephraim, that is, the people of Israel, recognizes that the idols are of no use: "O Ephraim, what have I to do anymore with idols?" Then God answers that he is the one who responds to his people and watches over them. He is compared to a flourishing cypress, a leafy tree that gives shade. Under his shade there is protection, and the fruit comes from him.

The one who speaks at the end is God, responding to Ephraim's repentance. Hosea closes his book with a promise of restoration after speaking of judgment and unfaithfulness. The verses before it show a people blossoming again. It is an invitation to return to God and to leave behind what once filled the heart.

For today: identify what has taken God's place in your life, such as money, fame, or fear. Say to him sincerely: "What have I to do anymore with this?" Return to him, and trust that from his care true fruit will grow in you.
exp.0:8:
God tells Hosea to name his third child Lo-ammi, which means "not my people." It is a harsh message: the people of Israel have turned away from God, and He declares that He no longer claims them as His own. "You" here refers to the nation as a whole.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, Israel, which lived in idolatry and unfaithfulness. The names of the prophet's children were living signs of that judgment. Yet the verses that follow announce hope: one day the people will be called "sons of the living God." Judgment is not the final word.

For today: God takes our faithfulness seriously, but His desire is to restore us. If you have wandered away from Him, do not remain in guilt; return to Him with confidence, for His mercy is greater than your failure.
exp.6:9:
Israel's arrogance stands as a witness that accuses them to their face. Even after hard things happened to them, they did not return to the LORD their God, and despite all this, they did not seek Him.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim. The people were weakened: foreign powers were wearing them down, and they did not even notice. Instead of turning back, they looked for help from Egypt and Assyria. God condemns their stubbornness and their spiritual blindness.

For today: pride can keep us from seeing our problems. When something in your life is wearing away, do not look first for human solutions. Humble yourself, return to God, and ask him to show you the truth with sincerity.
exp.4:7:
Blow the alarm of war in three towns of Benjamin: Gibeah, Ramah, and Beth-aven. The ram's horn and the trumpet were instruments that gave warning of danger. The battle cry "Lead on, O Benjamin!" can be understood as a call to the tribe to march out, or as a warning that the enemy is coming up behind them. Scholars interpret it in several ways. "Beth-aven" means "house of wickedness" and probably alludes to Bethel, where there was an idol.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had turned its back on him through its idolatry, and now judgment would come. The towns named were on the border, and the alarm warns that punishment is near.

For today: God warns us before the consequences arrive. If we notice that something has taken his place in our hearts, let us not wait until it is too late. Let us return to God today with sincerity, for he welcomes whoever repents.
exp.3:9:
They will eat, yet they will not be satisfied; they will be sexually immoral, yet they will not multiply. "Being satisfied" means being full and content, and "multiply" means having more children and growing in number. The reason given is plain: they have abandoned the Lord, that is, they have turned away from him, stopped listening to him, and stopped obeying him.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel. He accuses the priests and the people of living in wickedness and of profiting from the people's sin. Many understand the sexual immorality both literally and spiritually, because of the idolatry mentioned afterward. God warns that their actions will have consequences.

When we push God away from the center of life, we may have things and pleasures, yet we remain empty. Today we can ask ourselves what we are looking for to fill ourselves, and return to listening to God with humility.
exp.5:6:
This verse says that the people of Israel, like Adam, broke the covenant with God. "Transgressed" means stepping over a boundary, disobeying. "Unfaithful" means being disloyal and betraying a trust. "There" seems to point to a specific place, but it is not known which one.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He has just said that he desires mercy and the knowledge of God, not only offerings. The people kept the rituals, but their hearts were unfaithful. Some scholars read "like Adam" as a reference to the first man or to a place by that name, and they do not agree on which. Even so, the central idea is clear: they broke their promise to God.

For today: it is not enough to attend church or keep religious customs. God looks for a faithful heart and genuine love. Today you can check whether your relationship with him is sincere, and whether your treatment of others reflects the mercy he has shown you.
exp.13:1:
Hosea invites the people to return to God, but not empty-handed: "Bring your confessions," that is, honest words of sorrow for what they have done. He also teaches them what to say: "Take away all our iniquity" (forgive every sin) and "receive us graciously" (accept us kindly). The words "that we may present the fruit of our lips" describe offering praise and thanks to God in place of sacrifices.

The prophet Hosea speaks to the kingdom of Israel, which had turned away from God through idols and alliances with powers such as Assyria. After warning them of judgment, God himself opens a way back and even gives them the words to ask for forgiveness. The verses that follow show repentance: ceasing to trust in Assyria, in horses, and in idols, and trusting in God.

For today: when you have drifted away from God, do not wait until you feel perfect. Go to him with simple, honest words, ask for forgiveness, and trust in his mercy.
exp.12:15:
Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, will bear the consequences of its guilt because it rebelled against God. "Will be left in ruins" means it will be stripped bare and destroyed. "Fall by the sword" means they will die in battle. The verse describes the horror of war: the little ones will be dashed to pieces, and the pregnant women will be ripped open.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had abandoned God to follow Baal and to rely on alliances with other nations. Many understand that the punishment came through Assyria, around 722 B.C. These are cruel images that reflect the warfare customs of that time; the text does not say that God takes pleasure in them, but warns of the consequences of stubborn rejection.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he still offers forgiveness. If something is pulling you away from him, return today with humility, before the consequences grow.
exp.3:10:
What it says: Hosea says that promiscuity, wine, and new wine take away understanding. New wine is the fresh juice of the grape, still fermenting. To "take away understanding" means that these things rob a person of good judgment and clear thinking. In other words, these pleasures leave a person without the sense to decide well.

Context: God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel. The people and their priests had turned away from the LORD and mixed in with idolatry and the worship practices of neighboring peoples. God shows that this is not only a moral problem, but that their disordered desires made them unable to recognize Him.

For today: Examine what things are clouding your mind and pulling you away from God. When something takes away your clarity and your desire to seek Him, set limits and ask God and trusted people for help.
exp.9:14:
The verse says that Bethel will receive what it has done to others, because of its great wickedness. Bethel was the place where Israel worshiped idols, so the judgment falls on the very place that led the people astray. The verse also says that when the day dawns, the king of Israel will be completely cut off, which means the king will be removed entirely and without warning.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, Israel. The people trusted in their armies and in their own way, and they worshiped calves at Bethel. The message is clear: God warns of judgment for their idolatry and injustice.

Today we can ask ourselves what we truly trust in: our money, our strength, or our plans, or God. It is better to turn back to Him now, with humility, before we reap the bitter fruit of living far from Him.
exp.1:7:
God says that Israel, whom he calls "she," does not acknowledge that it was he who gave her the grain, the new wine, and the oil, that is, the basic food of each day. He also lavished on her silver and gold, but they used that gold to craft images for Baal.
