God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He compares Israel to an unfaithful wife who runs after other lovers, that is, the idols. She believes they are the ones who give her prosperity. For this reason God blocks her path, so that she will come to her senses and return to him.

For today: what we have, whether work, food, or money, comes from the hand of God. Before using it, give thanks. Ask yourself whether you are using it to honor him or whether it has become your main security.
exp.8:9:
God says that when He found Israel, it was like finding grapes in the middle of the desert: a joyful and refreshing surprise. He saw their ancestors as the firstfruits of the fig tree in its first season, sweet and eagerly awaited. But then they went to Baal-peor, a place where the false god Baal was worshiped, and they consecrated themselves to Shame. This means they turned away from God and ended up disgraced. They became as detestable as the thing they loved, just like the idol they chose.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom (Ephraim). He reminds them of the affection with which He chose them and contrasts it with their unfaithfulness. Baal-peor is mentioned in Numbers 25, when the people fell into idolatry and sin.

For today: what we worship shapes us over time. Let us ask God to help us love what is good and to return to Him, who looks on us with tenderness.
exp.1:15:
What the passage says: God promises that a day will come when his people will call him "my Husband," a name of love and closeness. They will no longer call him "my Master," a title of authority that the people had also used for Baal, the Canaanite god they had been worshiping instead of him.

Context: The Lord speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had gone after the Baals, like an unfaithful wife. Even so, God promises to lead her into the wilderness, speak tenderly to her heart, and restore the relationship. Scholars understand the wilderness as a time of starting over, though not all interpret it the same way.

For today: God does not seek only cold obedience, but a relationship of trust and love. Ask yourself whether anything occupies in your heart the place that belongs to God. If you have drifted away, he invites you to return and speak to him with sincerity.
exp.12:7:
God says that he will come against his people like a she-bear that has lost her cubs: furious and dangerous. He says he will attack them and tear open their chests, the place where life is held. Then he compares God to a lion that devours, and to a wild beast that tears its prey apart. It is a very strong image of judgment.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel. When the people had abundance, they grew proud and forgot their God. For this reason he announces punishment. Interpreters understand that the judgment would come through enemy nations, although here it is described with images of animals. Even so, the following verse leaves a door open: "in me is your help."

For today: when everything goes well for us, it is easy to forget God. Let us ask him for a humble and grateful heart, and let us return to him soon, for his correction seeks to rescue us.
exp.5:4:
Therefore I cut them down through the prophets; I killed them with the words of my mouth. God says that, because the people had grown hard, he sent his prophets to cut them down, that is, to strike them down and confront them, and that his words were like a sentence that kills. "Kill" here is strong language: God's word announces judgment. And those judgments go forth like lightning, bright and unmistakable, breaking into the open.

God speaks through Hosea. He has just said that the faithfulness of Ephraim and Judah, that is, their loyal love, is passing, like the morning cloud or the dew. Their repentance was shallow. Some understand that "hewn" refers to the harsh preaching of the prophets; the phrase is not entirely literal.

For today: it is not enough to feel sorry for a moment. Ask God for a steady heart, one that listens to his correction and turns it into daily obedience, not just passing emotion.
exp.6:10:
Hosea says that Ephraim, that is, the northern kingdom of Israel, was acting like a senseless dove. A frightened dove flies back and forth without any direction. In the same way, the people called out to Egypt for help and then turned toward Assyria.

The word "senseless" in the verse means foolish, or easy to deceive. The phrase "calling out to Egypt, then turning to Assyria" describes their restless movement from one foreign power to another.

Here God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel was being weakened by foreign nations, but did not realize it. Instead of returning to God, the people sought political alliances with neighboring powers. God warns them that this misplaced trust will bring their downfall, because they had turned away from the One who had redeemed them.

For today: when pressure, worry, or need comes, let us not run from one human solution to another without first seeking God. We may ask for advice and practical help, but our first look should go to Him, who is faithful and secure.
exp.6:4:
On the day of our king, the princes were inflamed with wine, and the king joined hands with people who mock what is sacred. The leaders of the land had drunk themselves into such a state that the king himself was drawn into their excess and ended up in league with scorners, those who make fun of what is holy.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom of Israel. He condemns its rulers for living in corruption, deceit, and excess, and for the fact that no one sought God. Scholars debate exactly which feast or king is meant, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: let us be careful about whom we keep company with and what things control us. Bad company and excess cloud our judgment and pull us away from God. Let us ask Him for wisdom and seek friends who encourage us to do what is right.
exp.9:4:
The people of Samaria will be afraid because of the calf of Beth-aven. Its people will mourn over it, and so will the idolatrous priests who used to rejoice in its glory, because the calf has been taken from them into exile. The calf is an image of a young bull that they worshiped. Beth-aven means "house of wickedness" and is used here as a nickname for Bethel.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom of Israel. The people had made false alliances and worshiped idols instead of trusting in the LORD. The verses that follow say that the calf will be carried off to Assyria as tribute. Some think this refers to a historical event that was close at hand; the text itself gives no further detail.

Whatever we put in place of God, whether money, success or reputation, cannot save us and can leave us weeping. Today, ask yourself: what gives me more security than God does? Give it to Him sincerely.
exp.3:7:
This verse says that the priests "feed on" the sins of the people, meaning they profit from them. The sin offerings were given to the priests (Leviticus 6:26). Here it seems that the priests benefit if the people keep on sinning, so that they receive more. The phrase "set their hearts on iniquity" means that they desire and long for that wickedness.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, in the northern kingdom of Israel. He accuses the priests of forgetting the law and not teaching the people. Therefore the people were perishing for lack of knowledge. Some interpreters see here a criticism of greed; the text gives no further detail.

For today: those who teach or lead others should seek the good of people, not their own gain. And all of us can ask ourselves: am I more interested in the truth of God or in what I gain from it? Let us ask God for a humble and faithful heart.
exp.3:11:
They consult wooden idols, as if a carved piece of wood could give them answers, and their divining rods seem to inform them. The phrase "divining rods" names sticks used to try to learn what lies ahead. "Prostitution" here refers to spiritual unfaithfulness: leaving God to follow other gods. That spirit leads them astray, and they have played the harlot against their God.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel, in the north. He accuses them of having stopped attending to the LORD and of practicing idolatrous worship on the mountains, under leafy trees. Some scholars think there were also sexual practices tied to those cults, although the details are debated.

Today we can look for answers in things that have no life or truth: horoscopes, fashions, or money. Better to seek God in prayer and in his Word, where there is sure guidance.
exp.12:6:
God himself, who once cared for Israel, will now come against them like a lion, and like a leopard that crouches beside the road. The word "watch" here means to wait and observe closely, ready for the right moment. The picture is not of a friendly animal, but of a danger close at hand.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom, Israel. He cared for them in the wilderness and gave them food, but when they were satisfied they became proud and forgot him. The images of wild beasts express judgment for that ingratitude, although the context ends by pointing out that help is found only in God.

For today: when everything is going well for us, it is easy to forget God. Today you can thank him for what you have and ask him for a humble heart, one that does not depend only on comfort.
exp.1:22:
God promises to plant his people in the land as a seed that he himself tends. He says he will have compassion on the one who had no compassion, and he will say to those called "Not My People," "You are My people." Then they will answer, "You are my God."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel, which had turned away from him through idolatry. The names of Hosea's children announced judgment, and here restoration is announced. After the discipline, God promises to begin again with his people.

For today: if you feel that you have failed or that you are far from God, remember that his compassion can change your story. Return to him with sincerity and say to him with confidence, "You are my God."
exp.10:2:
God says that he taught Ephraim, that is, Israel, to walk, like a father who holds his little child by the arms so that he can take his first steps. The phrase "taking them by the arms" shows how close and gentle that care was. But they never realized that it was God who was healing them.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He recalls how he loved Israel from the time he brought them out of Egypt, when they were like a child. Yet the people turned away after the Baals, false gods. The passage shows the pain of a father who cared for them tenderly and received no gratitude in return.

For today: we often receive help, protection and strength without noticing that they come from God. Today you can pause for a moment, remember how He has sustained you in the past, and give Him thanks sincerely.
exp.5:0:
It is an invitation to return to God. The verse opens with "Come," an urging to act now, and the call is to "return" to the LORD, to turn back toward him. The verse says that God "has torn us to pieces," which speaks of a painful judgment, and it also says that "He will heal us" and "bind up our wounds." The same God who wounded is the one who restores.

The speaker is the people of Israel, or someone urging them to repent, in a time of judgment and suffering. But in verse 4 God tells them that their love is passing, like the morning mist. For this reason some think this repentance was superficial, and others see it as a good example of turning back to God.

Today, when you go through pain or failure, do not run from God. Return to him with sincerity, trusting that he can heal what is broken.
exp.1:20:
He says that when the time of restoration comes, God himself will respond, and his response will set all of creation in motion. God responds to the heavens, the heavens respond to the earth, and the earth responds with the grain, the wine, and the oil. Here "respond" works like an echo: one thing answers another.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had been unfaithful to him, and God announces that he will again bind himself to his people with justice, mercy, and faithfulness. This promise shows that when the relationship with God is restored, order and provision are restored with it. Many understand it to point to a future blessing, and the details are interpreted in various ways.

For today: when you feel far from God or in need, draw near to him with confidence. He listens and responds, and his goodness often comes through simple, everyday things.
exp.12:5:
It says the people ate until they were full, and that once they were satisfied they became proud. That is why they forgot God. "Pasture" refers to the fields where livestock feed; here it suggests the blessings God gave them. "Satisfied" means eating until one is full. "Proud" means having an inflated sense of one's own importance.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel, also called Ephraim. He reminds them that He cared for them in the wilderness and that He alone is their Savior. But when they had abundance, they stopped depending on Him. The verses that follow announce a severe judgment, with images of wild beasts, as the consequence of that forgetfulness.

For today: when everything is going well, it is easy to feel that we do not need God. We can thank Him every day for what we have and remember that everything comes from His hand, so that abundance does not make us proud or forgetful.
exp.8:0:
God tells Israel not to rejoice or celebrate with exultation like the nations do. The reason is that the people had been unfaithful to God. Here, the phrase "played the harlot" means spiritual unfaithfulness, that is, worshiping other gods. The "love for hire" refers to the payment the people believed they were receiving from those idols. The "threshing floors" were the places where grain was separated from the stalks after the harvest.

The prophet Hosea speaks, sent by God to the northern kingdom of Israel (also called Ephraim). Many understand that the people credited their harvests to fertility gods, such as Baal, and not to the Lord. That is why it is announced that the harvest will fail and that there will be exile.

For today: check to whom you give credit for your blessings. Thank God, and do not place your trust in money or in success.
exp.2:4:
Afterward, Hosea says, after a long time without a king or proper worship, the people of Israel will return. They will seek the LORD their God and David their king. They will come trembling to the LORD and to His goodness, and the phrase "in the last days" points to a future time, which is understood in different ways.

Hosea is the prophet speaking. God had told him to love an unfaithful woman, as a picture of how Israel had been unfaithful to God. The verse before shows a time of waiting and discipline. Many Christians see in "David their king" a reference to Christ, a descendant of David, though others understand it in other ways.

Even when we have drifted away, God leaves the door open to return. If today you feel far from Him, seek Him sincerely and trust in His goodness.
exp.0:0:
This verse is the introduction to the book. It says that what follows is "the word of the LORD," meaning a message that God himself gave to Hosea, the son of Beeri. The phrase "came to Hosea" means that the word came to Hosea. Then it names the kings of Judah (Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah) and Jeroboam son of Jehoash, king of Israel, to place the message in time.

The one speaking is the author of the book, who presents Hosea as a prophet. We know nothing more about Beeri. The kings mentioned indicate that Hosea ministered over many years, in a time of instability and idolatry in Israel, the northern kingdom. Some scholars note that Jeroboam, the son of Jehoash, is the only king of Israel named, and they explain this in different ways.

For today: God speaks in real history, not in a vacuum. Before you offer your own opinion, ask him to speak to you through his Word, and obey it even when the moment is difficult.
exp.12:11:
It says that the wickedness of Ephraim is "bound up," meaning tied tight like a securely closed bundle, and that his sin is "stored up," meaning kept in reserve. God has not forgotten it. Ephraim was the leading tribe of the northern kingdom, Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He accuses Israel of having rejected his care and of having trusted in human kings. Their guilt does not vanish on its own, and judgment will come in its time. Even so, shortly afterward, the same chapter speaks of redemption and of victory over death.

For today: we cannot hide our sins or pretend they are already past. The wisest course is to bring them to God with sincerity and repentance, trusting that He forgives and sets free whoever returns to Him.
exp.6:1:
God says that the people do not stop to think that he remembers all their evil. The phrase "he remembers" means that God does not forget or overlook sin. The phrase "their deeds are all around them" means that their wrongdoing surrounds them like a wall they cannot escape, and everything they do is in plain view before God.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel, here called Ephraim, and its capital, Samaria, were living in deceit, injustice, and violence. God wanted to heal them, but as he drew near to them, their sin was laid bare. They believed no one could see them, and so they kept on in their wickedness.

For today: do not live as if what is hidden does not matter. God sees everything, but he also offers forgiveness. Tell him honestly today what you have kept silent about, and let him heal your heart.
exp.3:6:
It says that the more they grew in number, power and position, the more they sinned against God. The phrase "the more they multiplied" speaks of their growth or prosperity. The text says they exchanged their glory for something disgraceful. God is announcing that their honor will be turned into dishonor.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing above all the priests of Israel. They had the task of teaching the law, but they forgot it. Some understand the growth to refer to the increase of the priests; others, to the whole nation. In either case, the problem is that their privilege did not draw them closer to God, but pushed them away.

For today: when God gives us more success, influence or responsibility, it is wise to become more humble and more attentive to his Word. Blessings are not an excuse for neglecting God, but a reason to honor him more.
exp.5:10:
Judah is also said to have a harvest appointed for it, and that comes when God restores his people. The Hebrew word is usually rendered "harvest," so many versions read: "Also, O Judah, a harvest is set for you." The phrase "restore My people from captivity" means God bringing the people back to well-being.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He has just denounced the wickedness of Israel: violent priests, idolatry, and unfaithfulness. Now he includes Judah, the southern kingdom. There is debate over whether this harvest is one of judgment, because of their sins, or one of blessing, after restoration. Perhaps there is a bit of both.

For today: what we sow through our choices bears fruit sooner or later. But God, who corrects, also restores those who return to him. Today you can sow obedience and trust in him.
exp.7:6:
The verse says that Israel has sown the wind, meaning they have planted something empty and worthless, so they will reap the whirlwind, a violent storm of destruction. The wheat will not stand in the field, and what sprouts will fail to produce flour. Even if it should produce something, foreigners will consume it, swallowing it up.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom of Israel, also called Ephraim. The people had made idols, such as the golden calf at Samaria, and had turned to alliances with nations like Assyria instead of trusting in God. The text announces that these choices would end in loss and in rule by foreign powers.

For today: what we sow has consequences. If we place our trust in empty things, such as money, success, or the approval of others, we will reap more emptiness. Today you can sow in what lasts: prayer, honesty, and trust in God.
exp.8:1:
This verse says that the grain and the wine, which the people expected from their harvests, will no longer feed them. The threshing floor is the place where grain is beaten out, and the winepress is where grapes are trodden. The new wine is the fresh juice of the grape, and "will fail them" means that it will run out or not bear fruit.

The prophet Hosea speaks, sent by God to Israel. Some believe the people celebrated harvest festivals, attributing the abundance to false gods, and for this reason God calls this "whoredom," that is, being unfaithful to him. For this reason he warns them that their harvests will fail, as a consequence of their unfaithfulness.

For today: everything good we have comes from God, not only from our own effort. We can ask ourselves whether we are trusting in money or work more than in Him, and thank Him sincerely.
exp.1:14:
God promises to give back to his people their vineyards, meaning the abundance and blessing they had lost. The valley of Achor, which means "trouble," will become a gateway of hope. There the people will respond as they did in the days of their youth, as in the day they came up out of Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had been unfaithful, like a wife who runs after other lovers, chasing after the Baals. God corrects her, but he does not abandon her: he leads her into the wilderness to speak to her heart. The valley of Achor recalls Joshua 7, where there was sin and punishment; now God transforms it into hope.

For today: if you are going through a place of pain or failure, do not think it is the end. Return to God with sincerity. He can turn your valleys of trouble into gateways of hope and bring you back to the joy you once knew.
exp.10:11:
Hosea 11:12 says, in the Berean Standard Bible: "Ephraim surrounds Me with lies, the house of Israel with deceit; but Judah still walks with God and is faithful to the Holy One." Ephraim and Israel (the northern kingdom) surrounded God with falsehood in their dealings with him. Judah, for now, still walks with God.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He has just promised to restore his people, but he shows that they answered him with hypocrisy and lies. The last part is understood in several ways. Some believe it praises Judah, and others that it also corrects it.

For today: God looks for sincerity, not just religious words. Today you can pray openly, acknowledge your failures before him, and ask him for a faithful heart.
exp.3:13:
God says he will not punish the daughters for their prostitution or the daughters-in-law for their adultery, because the men themselves are doing worse: they go off with prostitutes and offer sacrifices alongside shrine prostitutes. "Punish" here means to call to account. "Prostitutes" are people who sell sex. "Shrine prostitutes" probably refers to women tied to the pagan cults. The verse concludes that a people without understanding will come to ruin.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel, which had given itself over to idolatry in the fertility cults. God shows them that the fathers and husbands are the main guilty parties, since they were setting the bad example. Some scholars think God here denounces the hypocrisy of men who blamed the women; others see it as a judgment in which God lets corruption run its course. Both readings are possible.

For today: those of us who lead others, as parents, leaders, or teachers, cannot demand what we do not live ourselves. Let us ask God for understanding and begin by examining our own hearts.
exp.7:4:
God says that the calf of Samaria, an idol, is something He rejects. The phrase "My anger burns against them" describes God's anger flaring against the people. The question "How long will they be incapable of innocence?" asks how long they will remain unable to be clean. The Hebrew text can be understood in two ways: that the calf drew them away from God, or that God rejected the calf. In both cases, the idol separates them from Him.

Hosea speaks to Israel, the northern kingdom, whose center was Samaria. God accuses them of setting up kings without consulting Him and of making idols out of their silver and gold. The calves recall the worship that Jeroboam established at Bethel and Dan. God warns that this path ends in ruin.

Today we can ask ourselves what we are putting in God's place: money, success, or security. Give it to Him sincerely, and ask Him to cleanse you and guide you.
exp.7:2:
Israel is said to have rejected what is good, that is, God and his ways. That is why an enemy will pursue them.

The people turned away from what was good and set it aside, so the consequences of that choice are described plainly: an enemy will chase them. The good they rejected can be understood as God himself, his instruction, and what is right.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom. The people had broken the covenant, made idols, and set up kings without consulting God. Earlier, the text already announces that judgment will come swiftly, like an eagle. God warns that turning away from him has consequences. Many scholars see Assyria as the enemy, although the text does not name it here.

Today we can ask ourselves which good things we have let slip: prayer, honesty, the Word. Saying "we know you" is not enough if we do not live according to it. Let us return to God today with simplicity and obedience.
exp.3:18:
A powerful whirlwind wraps Israel in its wings and carries her away, like someone being swept along who cannot resist. Their sacrifices to idols will only bring them shame, because they did them no good.

The prophet Hosea speaks, sent by God to the northern kingdom, called Ephraim. The people had given themselves over to idols and immorality, and their leaders sought bribes. Some understand "the wings" as the wings of the whirlwind itself; others see it as a picture of the judgment that would come upon them. In either case, the message is that their rebellion would end in ruin.

For today: examine what you place your trust in. If you seek security in anything other than God, sooner or later it will vanish like the wind. Return to Him with sincerity.
exp.1:1:
God invites the children to "rebuke" their mother, that is, to call her to account and confront her. She is Israel, seen as an unfaithful wife. God says that she is no longer his wife and that he is no longer her husband. He asks her to remove the adultery from her face and the unfaithfulness from between her breasts, that is, to put away her idolatry and disloyalty in plain sight of everyone.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, at a time when Israel was worshiping other gods. The children's names, Ammi, meaning "my people," and Ruhama, meaning "shown mercy," mean the call still carries hope. Many understand that the warning aims to lead the people to repentance, not only to punish them.

For today: if there is something in your life that has taken the place of God, do not hide it. Acknowledge it honestly, return to him, and seek help from mature brothers and sisters who will speak to you with truth and kindness.
exp.3:12:
The verse describes the people of Israel offering sacrifices on the mountaintops and hills and burning offerings there, under oak, poplar and terebinth trees, because their shade is pleasant. Burning offerings is the phrase the verse uses, so the offerings were made by fire. The verse then says that prostitution and adultery would follow, with daughters turning to prostitution and daughters-in-law to adultery. Here the verse speaks of sexual unfaithfulness. For this reason, God says, their daughters and daughters-in-law would fall into that same behavior.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, Israel. His people had abandoned the Lord to worship idols, and that worship was often mixed with sexual practices. Scholars explain in various ways how literal this was, but the text links it with spiritual unfaithfulness. The consequences reach the families.

For today: let us take care with what we worship and with what we do for comfort. What seems pleasant, like a good shade, can draw us away from God and affect our children. Let us live faithfully to God at home.
exp.9:7:
The high places of Aven, where Israel sinned, will be destroyed. Aven means "wickedness" or "emptiness," and it seems to be a scornful name for Bethel, the place where they set up a golden calf. Where there were once altars, thorns and thistles will overgrow them. In their terror, the people will cry out to the mountains, "Cover us!" and to the hills, "Fall on us!" That is, they would rather be crushed than face judgment.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim. The people had mixed the worship of God with idols and trusted in their king and their alliances. Hosea announces that Assyria would carry them into captivity and that their false refuges would not save them.

For today: examine the things you rely on more than God, such as money, success, or empty religiosity. Surrender them to Him today, before they collapse, and seek refuge in Him, who forgives the one who repents.
exp.9:9:
God says that he will discipline Israel whenever he chooses. Nations will gather against them and bring them into bondage because of their double transgression. The image is of a people brought under a heavy yoke for the guilt they have piled up.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim. The people had false altars and had turned away from God for a long time, and God announces that their sin would bring judgment.

For today: God corrects because he loves, and he calls us not to harden our hearts. If you notice something in your life that is pulling you away from God, do not wait for the consequence to arrive; seek the Lord now, with humility, and let him teach you the right path.
exp.12:0:
Hosea 13:1 says that the tribe of Ephraim, the largest in the northern kingdom, held great authority. When it spoke, there was trembling, which means people felt respect and fear. It was exalted, honored and lifted up in Israel. But it incurred guilt by worshiping Baal, a false god, and with that it died, left spiritually ruined and under judgment.

Here the prophet Hosea speaks on behalf of God, before the fall of the kingdom of Israel. Ephraim represents the whole northern kingdom. God reminds it of its former influence to show that the idol led it to ruin. The verses that follow show that the sin kept growing worse.

For today: a position, success, or the respect of others does not protect us if we place our hearts in something that is not God. It is worth examining what holds first place in our lives and humbly returning to Him.
exp.9:2:
It says that a time will come when the people of Israel will recognize that they have been left without a king. And it gives the reason: they did not revere the Lord, that is, they did not honor or obey him. Then, in discouragement, they ask what a king could possibly do for them. "Revere" here means honoring and respecting God.

The prophet Hosea is speaking, delivering God's message to the northern kingdom, Israel. Earlier, they were described as a vine that flourished, but they used their blessings to raise altars and idols. Hosea announces that judgment is coming, and that neither the king nor politics will be able to save them. Scholars understand this as an announcement of the fall of the northern monarchy.

For today: no leader, plan, or system can give us what comes only from a life surrendered to God. Ask him to order your heart before anything else.
exp.7:7:
He says Israel will be "swallowed up," meaning devoured or absorbed by other nations. Soon they will be among the nations like a worthless vessel, a broken pot that no one wants and that gets thrown away. The word "presto" is a Hebrew term meaning "soon," and the "nations" are the peoples around them.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. The northern people, called Israel or Ephraim, had abandoned God: they made a calf to worship in Samaria and sought protection from Assyria instead of trusting the Lord. God announces the consequences of that path. Historians connect this judgment with the fall of Samaria to Assyria, around 722 B.C.

For today: when we look for security in things that are not God, such as money, power, or alliances, we end up empty. Today you can ask yourself what you truly trust in and return your trust to the Lord, who truly sustains and gives worth to his people.
exp.9:8:
God reminds Israel that its sin goes back a long way, to the days of Gibeah. He says that Israel has "remained" there, meaning they kept on in the same wickedness without changing. The last question is hard: it asks whether the battle in Gibeah did not overtake the sons of iniquity back then, or whether it will overtake them now.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim. Gibeah recalls a terrible episode of wickedness and violence, told in Judges 19 to 21. God uses that memory to show that the people are repeating old sins, and for that reason judgment is coming.

For today: let us not take lightly the repeated sins we have carried for years. Today we can acknowledge before God an old habit, ask him for forgiveness, and seek help to change, trusting in his mercy.
exp.7:1:
Hosea 8:2 says that when trouble comes, Israel will cry out to God, "O our God, we know You!" It is a cry for help that sounds very confident.

The verse is spoken by God through the prophet Hosea. He has just announced that an enemy will come like an eagle against his house, because the people broke the covenant and rebelled against his law. That is why this cry is not sincere: they say they know him, but their lives contradict it. Later in the chapter we see that they had set up kings without consulting him and made idols.

For today: it is not enough to say "I know God" when problems arrive. Really knowing him shows in obeying him every day, not only in asking him for help during a crisis. Today you can ask yourself: does my life show what my mouth says?
exp.13:6:
They who return to God will dwell again in his shade and under his protection. They will grow grain and blossom like the vine, and their renown will be like the wine of Lebanon, a region known for its beauty and its fragrance. The verse does not say whether "his shade" refers to God's shade or to the shade of the restored people, and scholars read it in different ways.

Here God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had turned away from Him through idolatry and disobedience, but at the end of the book God promises to heal, forgive, and restore those who repent. The images of plants show new life after a time of dryness.

For today: if you feel dry or far from God, do not think that all is lost. Return to Him with sincerity, leave behind what pulls you away, and trust that His forgiveness can bring you life and fruit again.
exp.13:0:
It says that Israel must return to God, because its sin caused it to stumble. "Return" means turning back, changing course and coming back to Him. The verse's own wording carries the meaning: "Return" and "stumbled" are the key words here. God not only points out the stumble, He also invites them to get back up.

The prophet Hosea speaks, in God's name, to the people of Israel, the northern kingdom. This is the last chapter of the book, after many warnings about idolatry and lack of faithfulness. The verses that follow offer words for prayer: asking for forgiveness, not trusting in Assyria or in war horses, and giving up idols. It ends with the hope that God has mercy.

For today: if there is something in your life that drew you away from God, do not wait until you feel perfect. Go to Him today with a sincere prayer, acknowledge your mistake, and trust in His mercy.
exp.6:13:
God says that his people did not truly turn to him. They wailed while lying on their beds, but it was not a sincere cry from the heart. They slashed themselves only to get grain and new wine, that is, food and drink. The word "wail" describes loud, mournful crying, and "slash themselves" may refer to cutting the body as part of a ritual to ask for harvests. Meanwhile, they kept turning away from God.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the kingdom of Israel (also called Ephraim), in the 8th century BC. He accuses them of hypocrisy: they say it with their mouths, but their hearts are far away. Some interpret the slashing as rituals tied to gods of rain and harvest, though the text does not fully make this clear.

Today we can ask ourselves why we pray. It is good to ask for bread and provision, but God wants our hearts, not only his gifts. Let us seek today to know him, not only to receive from him.
exp.2:1:
So Hosea obeys God and buys this woman. He pays fifteen shekels of silver, along with a homer and a lethech of barley. A homer was a large measure of grain. Some think the total was a price similar to that of a slave, but this is not certain.

God speaks to the prophet Hosea. He tells him to love an adulterous woman, and the text suggests she is his wife Gomer. Her story is a picture of God's love for Israel, which had turned away to other gods, yet whom God did not abandon.

For today: God seeks us out and rescues us even when we have failed him. Receiving that love invites us to return to him with humility. It also encourages us to treat with patience and grace those who have failed us, without ignoring the truth.
exp.9:11:
God invites his people to sow righteousness and reap the fruit of loving devotion, that is, to live uprightly and receive the blessing of faithful love in return. "Break up your unplowed ground" means working land that has long lain untouched, in other words, opening a hardened heart. "It is time to seek the LORD" means that the opportunity is now, until he comes and sends righteousness down on you like rain.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel, called Ephraim. The people had trusted in their own strength and their idolatry, and for this judgment was coming. Even so, before the punishment, God offers them a way out: to return to him with humility and sincerity.

Today we can ask ourselves what area of our life has become hardened. With humility, let us set aside time to pray and read the Bible, and begin to practice justice and kindness in some concrete way, without waiting for tomorrow.
exp.5:2:
This verse says the people want to know God and to keep pressing on to know him every day. It compares God to the sunrise, which comes up with certainty, and to the rain that waters the earth. The comparison to spring showers fits the picture of rain that brings growth to the land and fields.

Here the people of Israel speak, urging one another to return to God after the punishment. But in the verses that follow, God answers that their love is like a morning cloud and dew that soon passes away. In other words, the words sound good, but the heart was not yet steady.

For today: knowing God is not a passing emotion but a daily path. Set aside a regular time to read his Word and pray, and let that faith show in your conduct, not only in your words.
exp.0:5:
This verse tells us that Gomer had another daughter, and God told Hosea to name her "Lo-ruhamah," which means "Not Pitied" or "No Mercy." God says that He will no longer have compassion on the house of Israel, that He should ever forgive them. The phrase in the Berean Standard Bible is "I will no longer have compassion on the house of Israel, that I should ever forgive them," so the name points to a withdrawal of mercy rather than a simple absence of pity.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, who lived in the northern kingdom of Israel in a time of idolatry and injustice. The names of his children were living messages for the people. This name warned of a coming judgment. But the next verse shows that God would still have mercy on Judah, and that their salvation would not come by military strength, but by Him.

For today: God's mercy is a gift, not a right we can take for granted. Let us take the opportunity today to turn back to Him sincerely, instead of trusting in our own resources.
exp.3:1:
This verse describes the sins of the people. "Cursing" means speaking evil against others or against God; "lying" means saying what is untrue; "murder" means killing another person; "stealing" means taking what belongs to someone else; and "adultery" means being unfaithful in marriage. The verse says these evils are rampant, meaning they have become common and widespread. "One act of bloodshed follows another" describes violence that keeps coming, with no pause between one killing and the next.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to Israel, the northern kingdom. He brings a charge against them, as in a courtroom, because they had abandoned truth, mercy, and the knowledge of God. The verses that follow show that this sin also harmed the land and its creatures.

For today: when we truly know God, it shows in everyday life. Today you can choose one concrete action, such as keeping your word or being honest even when it costs you, in order to live with truth and mercy.
exp.0:7:
This verse tells us that Gomer, the wife of the prophet Hosea, stopped nursing their daughter Lo-ruhamah and became pregnant again. A son was born. "Weaned" means that the child no longer drank breast milk, which suggests that a few years had passed. To give birth is to bring a child into the world.

God spoke to Hosea, and the life of his family became a message for Israel. The name Lo-ruhamah means "not pitied," and it showed that the northern kingdom had fallen into idolatry and would soon face judgment. The next child will be given the name Lo-ammi, "not my people." But the passage ends with hope: God promises to restore his people.

For today: even when our mistakes have consequences, God does not stop speaking to us with hope. We can return to him sincerely, trusting that his mercy is greater than our past.
exp.9:3:
They talked a great deal, but their words were empty. They made agreements and swore oaths they never meant to keep. So God's judgment would spring up like poisonous weeds in the furrows of a field, where good fruit should have grown.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom (Israel, also called Ephraim). The people had a divided heart: they worshiped idols and trusted in kings and human alliances, not in the LORD. Their broken agreements with others and with God brought injustice and judgment as a result.

For today: take care with your words and your promises. If you say you will do something, keep it with honesty, above all before God. A life of empty words produces bitter fruit, but sincerity and faithfulness build trust and honor the Lord.
exp.2:0:
This verse tells how God speaks to Hosea again and commands him to show love to his wife, who is loved by another man and is an adulteress. God compares this love with his own love toward Israel, a people who turn to other gods. "Raisin cakes" offered to idols probably refers to the same sweet offerings used in pagan worship, though some understand the phrase simply as a love of pleasure.

The Lord is speaking, and Hosea is the prophet. God uses Hosea's married life as a living sign: just as Hosea is to love an unfaithful wife, God continues to love his unfaithful people. It is not known with certainty whether this woman is Gomer, the one from Hosea 1, and scholars interpret this in different ways.

For today: God's love does not depend on our faithfulness. You can return to Him with confidence, and you can also strive to love with patience those who have failed you.
exp.9:5:
It says that the wooden idols Israel worshiped at Beth-aven will be carried to Assyria as tribute for the great king. Israel will be ashamed of its wooden idols, which means its own chosen gods will bring it disgrace. Ephraim, who stands for the northern kingdom, will be seized with shame.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, which trusted in idols and in alliances with other nations instead of trusting in Him. The verse does not name the great king, and scholars understand the figure in several ways.

For today: whatever we put in place of God, whether money, power, or our own plans, ends up failing and leaving us ashamed. Let us ask God to guide our decisions and trust Him first.
exp.11:10:
God says that he himself spoke to the prophets, that he gave them many visions and messages, and that through them he used parables or examples so that the people would understand. "I multiplied prophecy" means that he sent word after word, again and again.

Here God speaks to the people of Israel, who are called Ephraim, and who boasted of their wealth and believed themselves free of blame. God reminds them that he has been their God since Egypt and that they have not lacked warning. The verses that follow show that, even so, the people kept on in idolatry, offering sacrifices at Gilgal and building altars across the fields.

For today: God continues to speak with clarity, and it is not his fault if we do not listen. Before trusting in what we have achieved, it is wise to open the Bible with humility and let God correct us.
exp.1:16:
It says that God will remove from the mouths of his people the names of the Baals, meaning the false gods they worshiped. After that, their names will no longer be spoken or called upon.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had been unfaithful to him, going after the Baals, Canaanite gods tied to rain and harvest. Hosea uses the image of a broken marriage. Here God promises to restore his people. They used to call him "Baali," which could mean "my lord" or "my Baal," but God wants them to call him "my husband," with affection and faithfulness.

For today: God does not only forgive, he also heals the heart. We can ask ourselves what things have taken God's place in our lives and ask him to help us let them go, so that his name becomes the one we speak most often with love and trust.
exp.11:2:
This verse says that the LORD has a case against Judah, a charge or legal dispute. He is going to call Jacob to account, which here means asking for an account of his conduct. "According to his ways" means according to his way of living. The next phrase means that God will repay them according to what they have done.

The prophet Hosea, a messenger of God, speaks in a time of deceit and political alliances with Assyria and Egypt. Some think Judah receives a warning even though it was praised earlier; others see a reference to the whole nation. The text allows both readings.

For today: God sees our way of living, not only what we say. Today you can examine your decisions and return to Him with sincerity, trusting in His mercy.
exp.0:6:
God says he will have mercy on Judah, the southern kingdom, and will save them by the LORD their God, that is, through Himself. He will not rescue them by bow or sword or war, or by horses and cavalry. The verse's "save them" is the same phrase as "I will save them," and the cavalry in view are the horsemen of war.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He has just announced judgment on Israel, the northern kingdom, for its unfaithfulness, and he shows it through the name of the daughter, Lo-ruhamah, "not pitied." This verse contrasts with that: Judah will receive compassion. Many connect it with the deliverance of Jerusalem from Assyria in the time of Hezekiah (2 Kings 19), although the text does not say so in those words.

For today: do not place your security only in your resources, your preparation, or your strength. Do your part responsibly, but rest in the fact that salvation and mercy come from God, and return to Him with confidence.
exp.1:0:
This verse says that the people are to call their brothers "My people" and their sisters "My loved one." These names reverse the earlier message.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to Israel, the northern kingdom. Earlier, the children had been given names of rejection: "Not my people" and "Not loved." Now God announces that he will again call them his own. Some understand this as foreshadowing restoration after the punishment. The New Testament cites this idea to speak of grace that reaches everyone (Romans 9:25-26; 1 Peter 2:10).

For today: if you feel far from God because of your failures, remember that his mercy can change your story. And encourage others to believe that God still calls them his own.
exp.7:12:
This verse says that the people offered sacrifices to God and ate the meat, but God did not accept them. The words "remember their iniquity" and "punish their sins" mean that he will hold them accountable for their wrongs. "They will return to Egypt" means they will go back to a situation like slavery; some understand this literally and others as a picture of punishment and exile.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Ephraim or Israel. They built many altars and performed many rituals, but they ignored God's law and had forgotten him. Their religion was outward show, without obedience or sincere love.

For today: it is not enough to keep rituals, go to church, or give offerings if the heart is far from God. Ask him to teach you to obey him truly, with humility and sincerity, not merely out of habit.
exp.9:6:
It says that the king of Samaria will be carried off and destroyed suddenly, and that he will vanish like a twig on the surface of the water. He seems to be something, but a current sweeps him away without leaving a trace. The image is one of something light and fragile, unable to stay where it is.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, Israel, whose capital was Samaria. The people trusted in their kings and in the golden calves at Bethel, a false worship. God announces that neither the throne nor the idols will be able to save them, and that Assyria will defeat them.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security: in power, money, or leaders, who pass away like a twig on the water. Only God is firm. Let us trust first in Him.
exp.8:11:
God says that even if the children of Ephraim (the kingdom of Israel) are raised, he will take each one from them, so that they will vanish or die. Then he adds, with grief, "Woe to them" when he turns away from them.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Earlier he recalls how he delighted to find Israel, like grapes in the wilderness, but they gave themselves over to idolatry at Baal-peor. Because of this, judgment comes: their families and their future will be affected. Some scholars see here a warning of war and exile, though the text itself gives no further detail.

For today: the worst punishment is living far from God. Do not take your relationship with him lightly. Return to God with sincerity, and pray for your family so that it grows under his care.
exp.12:3:
God reminds the Israelites who he is: the LORD their God, who brought them out of Egypt, and the only God they have. He tells them they must not acknowledge any other god, because there is no Savior besides him. In the verse, "Yet" marks a turn in the message, and "besides Me" means "apart from Me."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, Israel. The people had made idols of silver, including calves they kissed in worship. God calls to mind their history: he freed them from Egypt and cared for them in the wilderness. Their error was forgetting the one who had saved them and trusting in things made by human hands.

For today: ask yourself what you are trusting in to feel secure, such as money, work, or the approval of others. Those things cannot save you. Remember how God has sustained you in other times, and place your trust in him again.
exp.8:14:
All their evil is seen at Gilgal, for there God came to hate them. Because of the evil of their deeds, he says he will drive them out of his house (probably the land or the covenant family), and he will no longer love them. "Leaders" here refers to their rulers, who are rebellious, meaning they revolt against God.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, also called Ephraim. Gilgal was an important place in its history, but here it is associated with idolatry and sin. It is not known with precision what event is meant; scholars explain it in several ways. God makes this announcement of judgment because the people and their leaders rejected his covenant.

For today: it is not enough to have places, rituals, or religious activities if the heart turns away from God. Ask him to examine your heart, and if there is something that does not please him, return to him with sincerity. His judgment is serious, but it always invites repentance.
exp.11:11:
The passage says that Gilead is full of wickedness, and that what the people do there is worthless, something empty. In Gilgal they offered bulls as sacrifices, yet their altars will end up like piles of stones in the furrows of a plowed field. The question "Is Gilead iniquity?" can be understood in several ways, and scholars put it in different ways.

The verse belongs to a passage where God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel, also called Ephraim. Hosea has already recalled how God brought the people out of Egypt and sent them prophets. Gilead and Gilgal were places of worship, and it seems that religion there had become empty, mixed with idols and without sincere obedience.

For today: performing religious acts is not enough if the heart is far from God. Ask yourself whether your faith shows in the way you live, in justice and in obedience, and not only in what you do on Sundays.
exp.6:8:
Verse 9 says that foreign peoples have been consuming the strength and wealth of Ephraim (the northern kingdom, Israel), and he has not even noticed. Gray hair has also appeared on him, a sign that he was growing weaker and aging, and he did not notice that either. "Strength" here means force or resources, and "gray hair" points to the gray hair itself, that is, to the wear and decline.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel was seeking alliances with other nations instead of calling on God, and those alliances were wearing it down. Some think this refers to tribute paid to Assyria; the text does not spell this out. The central point is spiritual blindness: he was declining and did not recognize it.

For today: sometimes sin, carelessness, or bad habits wear us down little by little without our noticing. Let us ask God to show us honestly where we stand, and return to Him soon, before the damage grows.
exp.4:14:
God says that he will withdraw and return to his place, meaning he will step away from them, until they admit their guilt and earnestly seek him. The phrase "I will return to My place" means he will go away, and "they will earnestly seek Me" means they will look for him eagerly and urgently when they are in trouble.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom (Ephraim) and also to Judah. They trusted in Assyria and not in God, and he warns them that no human king will be able to heal them. His withdrawal works as discipline, with the hope of leading them to repentance. Some understand this as the exile that would come; the text gives no further details.

For today: when you feel that God is silent or things are becoming difficult, do not rush first to other ways out. Examine your heart, admit whatever needs to be admitted, and seek him with sincerity. He receives those who return to him.
exp.3:3:
It says that no one should argue with or accuse another, because the problem is not in this one or that one, but in the whole people. "Contend" means to fight or dispute, and "offer reproof" means to correct or accuse. The people are compared to those who oppose the priest, that is, they reject the one who was supposed to teach them the law of God.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He has just accused Israel of lying, stealing, murdering and committing adultery. Here he seems to say that blaming one another no longer helps, since everyone is responsible. Some scholars also understand that the priest is being accused, as is seen later; the verse is difficult and is understood in several ways.

For today: before pointing out the faults of others, examine your own heart. Acknowledge your part, seek the Word of God with humility, and let it correct you first.
exp.11:8:
Ephraim, which stands for the northern kingdom of Israel, takes pride in its wealth. It says it became rich through its own hard work and that no one can point to any wrongdoing or sin in everything it has earned.

God, speaking through the prophet Hosea, addresses a people who trust in their money. The verse before this one describes false scales and the oppression of others, so Ephraim regards itself as innocent even while it cheats. God reminds it that He is the Lord its God, who has been with it since the land of Egypt, and that He had sent prophets to correct it.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we measure our honesty only by what we achieve. Being successful does not prove that we act rightly. It is wise to examine with humility how we earn our money, and to thank God for what we have.
exp.12:8:
The verse reads: "You are destroyed, O Israel, because you are against Me—against your helper." The phrase "You are destroyed" means that Israel brought ruin upon itself through its own choices. Even so, God leaves a door open: the only true help comes from Him.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to Israel, the northern kingdom, which had turned away from Him to follow idols and to trust in human kings. Earlier, God had described His judgment with fierce images of wild beasts. Afterward He asks where the king is in whom they trusted. Some interpreters read that question as a rebuke, and others as a promise of help despite the punishment.

For today: when your mistakes have left you with no way out, do not blame others or sink into despair. Acknowledge your responsibility and return to God, who continues to offer His help to anyone who asks for it.
exp.8:13:
Here the prophet Hosea asks God what he should give Israel, and then he answers in God's voice: "Give them wombs that miscarry and breasts that dry up!" The request is harsh. Losing the ability to bear children, and to nurse them, would take away one of the greatest blessings a people could have.

Hosea speaks to Ephraim, the name of the northern kingdom, Israel. They had fallen into idolatry, and the text names Gilgal as a place of their wickedness. Children were a sign of blessing, so losing them would be a very painful judgment. Some think Hosea says this with grief, not with pleasure, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he also does so with pain. Let us examine whether we are letting something take the place of God, and return to him with humility while there is still time.
exp.9:10:
Ephraim, the northern kingdom of Israel, is compared to a well-trained heifer that loves to thresh grain, an easy job that let her eat as she walked. But God says he will place a yoke on her fair neck, meaning her strong and well-kept neck, and will harness Ephraim. Then Judah will plow and Jacob will break up the hard ground, hard labor in the field.

It is God speaking, through the prophet Hosea. Israel had lived at ease and trusted in its own strength, but it had turned away from God for a long time. The yoke announces discipline and the loss of freedom. Some understand that "Judah" and "Jacob" also show that the whole people would be reached; the text allows several readings.

For today: spiritual comfort can make us drowsy. Examine where you have stopped obeying God because you feel settled, and seek him again today, before life demands it of you by force.
exp.13:3:
God promises to heal the apostasy of his people. "I will heal" describes God's restoring work, and "their apostasy" is their turning away from him. The promise to love them freely is here rendered as "I will freely love them," and the phrase "my anger has turned away from them" means that his anger has already passed.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had turned away from him, trusting in Assyria, in their war horses, and in their idols. But God invites them to return with sincere words of repentance, and here he answers with a promise of forgiveness and restoration.

For today: when you fail or have wandered away from God, do not hide yourself or try to fix it alone. Return to him with honesty, confess your fault, and receive his forgiveness. God does not only forgive; he also heals the depths of the heart and loves you generously.
exp.11:1:
Ephraim, the northern kingdom of Israel, "feeds on the wind." That means it chases something that gives no nourishment and bears no fruit. The hot, dry east wind that destroys crops is what the wind stands for here. Ephraim multiplies lies and ruin, because it makes deals with Assyria and sends oil to Egypt, probably as payment or a gift to win political support.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea in the eighth century B.C. Israel trusted in alliances with the great powers instead of trusting the Lord. God calls this deceit and disloyalty. Judah appears to be in a better position at that moment, though the following text shows that it too will be called to account. The verse says the Lord has a charge to bring against Judah, and that he will punish Jacob according to his ways and repay him according to his deeds.

For today: when anxiety pushes us to seek security in money, influence, or empty promises, it is wise to stop and ask whether these things truly sustain us. Trusting God and asking him for direction is firmer ground than chasing the wind.
exp.6:11:
As they go, I will spread my net over them, the way one catches birds, and bring them down. I will punish them when I hear them flocking together.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel, like a naive dove, ran from Egypt to Assyria looking for protection, instead of returning to God. He had redeemed them, yet they answered him with lies and sought him only for grain and wine. Some understand the flocking together as the warnings God had already given them; the text allows other readings.

For today: when pressure comes, let us not run first to everything else. Let us seek God sincerely, not only when we need something.
exp.6:12:
God speaks with grief as well as anger: "Woe to them!" The people have strayed from him and rebelled against him. "Destruction" names the ruin that follows from turning away. God says he would have redeemed them, meaning he would have rescued them, as he did when he brought them out of Egypt. Yet they speak lies against him, dealing falsely with him and failing to keep what they promised him.

Here God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Ephraim. Like a naive dove, Israel was seeking help from Egypt and Assyria instead of from God. So the Lord announces that he will catch them like birds in a net. Many understand their lies to include a religion without heart, as the following verse suggests.

For today: do not look for security only in human resources while ignoring God. Remember what he has done for you, and call on him sincerely, not only when you need grain and new wine.
exp.10:7:
Here God asks himself: "How could I give you up, Ephraim? How could I surrender you, Israel?" Admah and Zeboiim were cities destroyed along with Sodom, and God says he could never treat his people that way. "My heart is turned within Me" and "My compassion is stirred" mean that his compassion rises with great force inside him.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Ephraim is another name for the northern kingdom, Israel. The people had rebelled, and punishment was approaching. Even so, God shows a tension between his justice and his love, and in the end his compassion has the final word.

For today: if you have failed, do not run from God thinking he has already rejected you. His discipline does not come from contempt but from a love that does not let you go. Return to him sincerely and trust in his mercy.
exp.5:7:
Gilead is a city of evildoers, tracked with footprints of blood. This verse says that Gilead was a city full of people who did evil, and that its streets were marked by violence and bloodshed. "Evildoers" are those who deliberately do wrong, and "footprints of blood" pictures violence and unjust killings left behind wherever they walked.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea and accuses the people of the northern kingdom, Israel. Earlier he said that he wanted mercy and the knowledge of him, not only offerings. Scholars are not sure which exact event is meant here, nor which city in the region of Gilead is in view. But the message is clear: their religion was not changing their conduct.

For today: going to church or keeping rituals is not enough. Ask God that your faith show in how you treat others, with justice, respect, and mercy.
exp.6:6:
The whole people is set on fire like an oven, full of passions and schemes. In their rage they devour their rulers, and one after another their kings fall. The saddest part is that, in the middle of so much crisis, not one of them calls upon God. The comment about "devoured" has been adapted to the verse above: the word "devour" means they consume their rulers.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim. There were conspiracies, drunkenness, and political murders. God complains that, even with so much chaos, the people do not turn back to seek him.

For today: when everything falls into disorder in our lives or around us, let us not trust only in human solutions. Before acting out of anger or ambition, let us pause and call upon God sincerely. He remains attentive to those who seek him.
exp.0:10:
God promises that the people of Judah and the people of Israel, two peoples divided for a long time, will be gathered together again. They will appoint for themselves one leader, and they will go up out of the land. This may mean they will return from exile, or it may point to a picture of growth, since Jezreel means "God sows," and the people will spring up like a sown crop. The day of Jezreel will be great: a day of restoration.

Hosea writes to the northern kingdom, which had been unfaithful to God. The names of his children, such as Lo-ammi ("not my people"), announced judgment. But God, who is speaking, adds hope: rejection will not be his final word. Some Christians see in that leader a reference to Christ; others think first of a king from the line of David.

For today: if you feel far from God or divided from others, remember that God knows how to gather and heal. Ask him today to help you take one concrete step toward reconciliation.
exp.12:13:
God promises to rescue his people from the power of the grave and from death. The grave is the place of the dead. He asks where death's plagues are and where the grave's sting is, which means he is claiming victory over both. The final phrase, "compassion is hidden from My eyes," is harder to read. It means that God will not turn away from his promise, and his mercy stays fixed on his people.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Before and after this verse, he announces judgment on Ephraim (Israel) for its sin. In the middle of the punishment appears this promise of hope. Scholars debate whether it speaks of a nearby deliverance, the restoration of Israel, or the final resurrection. The apostle Paul uses similar words in 1 Corinthians 15:55 when speaking of victory over death.

Today, when you feel fear about death, a loss, or your own failures, remember that God has the last word. Trust his promise and live with hope.
exp.1:21:
There is a chain of responses in this verse: God responds to the heavens, the heavens respond to the earth, and the earth responds with grain, new wine, and oil, the basic foods of the people. In the end, all that growth responds to Jezreel. Jezreel means "God sows."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had been unfaithful to him, and because of that there was punishment. But here God promises to restore the relationship, like a husband who takes his wife back. Jezreel, which once sounded like judgment, now becomes an image of blessing and sowing. Scholars interpret it in several ways, but all see a promise of renewal.

For today: when you feel your life is dry because of your failures, remember that God can restore. Return to him with confidence, and wait for his provision step by step.
exp.7:13:
Israel has forgotten the one who made him, and who formed him into a nation. Instead of trusting in God, he has built palaces, and Judah has filled the land with fortified cities. God answers that he will send fire upon those cities, and it will consume their citadels.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom of Israel and also Judah. The people had God's law, but they treated it as something foreign. Their religion was only ritual, and they trusted in political and military security. God calls them to account for abandoning their relationship with him.

For today: examine where you place your security. Houses, savings, work, or religious activities can become a substitute for God. Set aside time each day to remember that he is your Creator and to obey him sincerely.
exp.9:0:
Israel is compared here to a luxuriant vine, full of growth. But that vine bore fruit for itself, that is, for its own benefit. The more its fruit increased, the more altars it built for its idols. The "sacred pillars" were stones or pillars used in pagan worship. The better the land produced, the more the people gave themselves over to idolatry.

Here the prophet Hosea speaks, sent by God to the northern kingdom, Israel, shortly before its fall. God denounces that the people used their blessings to worship idols and not Him. The following verse says that their heart was divided and that God would tear down those altars.

For today: blessings should draw us closer to God, not push us away. Ask yourself whether, when things go well for you, your gratitude and your service to God grow, or whether you begin to trust more in your achievements and possessions.
exp.7:9:
Verse 10 says that even though Israel hires allies from among the nations, God will round them up, meaning he will bring them under judgment. Israel will begin to diminish under the oppression of the king of princes. The phrase "hire allies" means paying or contracting for help; the "nations" are the peoples around them; "diminish" means losing strength and standing under pressure.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel, also called Ephraim, sought political protection in Assyria and paid for alliances instead of trusting God. Many understand "round them up" as a reference to judgment: those same powers would turn against them. The text does not spell out all the historical details.

For today: when you are afraid, do not buy security with things that pull you away from God. Pray first, seek wise counsel, and trust that He cares for you better than any human alliance.
exp.1:2:
It says that God warns what he would do if she does not give up her unfaithfulness: he would strip her of everything, expose her as on the day she was born, and make her like a desert, a parched land, and she would die of thirst. "Strip" means to take away everything one has. "Return" means to go back to an earlier state. "Plead" means to bring a formal complaint or charge.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He compares Israel to an unfaithful wife who looks for other lovers, that is, the idols, and credits them with the bread, the water, and the wool, when all of it comes from God. The names Lo-ammi ("not my people") and Lo-ruhamah ("not pitied") call the children to plead with their mother. The warning aims to make her react and return.

For today: ask yourself where you really expect your security and your provision to come from. Thank God for what you have, and do not place your trust in things that cannot sustain you.
exp.11:0:
Ephraim, the northern kingdom, and the whole house of Israel surround God with lies and deceit. Judah, by contrast, still stands with God and is faithful. This last phrase is hard to translate, and readers will find that the wording varies, with some explaining it as Judah walking with God or remaining loyal to him. Scholars also debate whether the reference to the holy ones means God himself or his faithful people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel claimed to worship him, but it sought security in alliances with Assyria and Egypt and lived in falsehood. God confronts them with sorrow. Judah fares better for now, though the text that follows shows that God also has a case against her.

Today we might ask whether we are sincere with God or only go through the motions outwardly. Trusting him with honesty is worth more than leaning on our own plans.
exp.0:9:
Says that, despite the punishment announced, the people of Israel will become too many to count, like the sand of the sea. And in the very place where God said to them, "You are not My people," one day they will be called "sons of the living God." "Yet" means "even so."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Earlier, the names of his children, Lo-ruhama ("not pitied") and Lo-ammi ("not My people"), announced judgment for Israel's unfaithfulness. Here the message changes: judgment is not the final word. This recalls the promise made to Abraham about his descendants. The New Testament quotes this passage in Romans 9:25-26, applying it also to people from all nations.

For today: if you feel that your failures have left you far from God, remember that His mercy can change your story. Return to Him with confidence, and let Him call you His son or daughter.
exp.9:1:
The verse says that Israel's heart was devious: they were not fully faithful to God. Because of this, they must now bear their guilt. "The LORD" most likely refers to God, who will break down the altars and demolish the sacred pillars they used to worship. The verse describes this judgment as a ruin, leaving their places of worship torn down and broken.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, Israel. When the land gave them abundance, instead of thanking God, they multiplied altars and pillars. They used their blessings to serve themselves and other gods. Some interpreters also see here a reference to the king, but the general sense of the judgment is clear.

Today we can ask ourselves: do the blessings God gives me bring me closer to Him, or do they distract me from Him? A devious heart does not find peace. Ask God to help you love Him wholeheartedly and to be thankful in abundance.
exp.3:2:
Therefore, it says, because of the people's sins, the land will mourn. Everyone who lives in it will waste away, along with the beasts of the field and the birds of the air. Even the fish of the sea will disappear.

The word "mourn" here means that the land will be sad, as at a funeral. The word "waste away" means that they will grow weak and fade. The word "disappear" means that they will be gone.

Here God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel. God brings an accusation against his people because there was no longer any truth, mercy, or knowledge of him, and lying, stealing, adultery, and violence were everywhere. Many understand that creation suffers because of human wickedness. Some think the text refers to drought or to ruin from an invasion; the text does not spell this out.

Today, this verse reminds us that our choices affect other people and the world around us. We can seek God, live with honesty, and show mercy, caring for creation as well.
exp.3:14:
Hosea 4:15 says that even though Israel, the northern kingdom, has given itself over to spiritual unfaithfulness, Judah, the southern kingdom, should take care not to fall into the same thing. He warns them not to journey to Gilgal or go up to Beth-aven, places of corrupted worship, and not to swear on oath, "As surely as the LORD lives," while they mix their worship with idols. "Prostitute yourself" here speaks of unfaithfulness to God; "Beth-aven" means "house of wickedness" and is probably a way of referring to Bethel, "house of God."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea in the eighth century B.C. He accuses Israel of mixing faith with idolatrous rites. He wants to keep Judah from following that same path.

For today: saying religious words is not enough when the heart is divided. Examine which places, habits, or influences pull you away from God, and step away from them before they carry you off. Being sincere with God matters more than looking spiritual.
exp.12:1:
The verse says that they keep on sinning more and more. They make cast images for themselves out of their silver, idols skillfully made, all of them the work of craftsmen. About them people say, "They offer human sacrifice and kiss the calves!" This verse says that the people of Israel kept on sinning. With their silver they made statues of cast metal, idols crafted with skill by workers. People also said of these images that they offered human sacrifice and kissed the calves, that is, worshiped those images. "The craftsmen" are the artisans who shaped them.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Ephraim, the leading tribe of the northern kingdom, had once been respected, but it became corrupted by the worship of Baal. God denounces that, instead of trusting in Him, they made gods with their hands. The verses that follow show that this idolatry would lead them to vanish like the morning mist, and God reminds them that only He is the Savior.

Today we may not kiss statues, but we can place our trust in money, success, or an image of God made to our own measure. Ask yourself: what occupies the place of God in my heart? Surrender it to Him in prayer today and return to trusting in Him.
exp.12:10:
God speaks: "So in My anger I gave you a king, and in My wrath I took him away."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel (Ephraim). He reminds them that they asked for a human king to feel secure (1 Samuel 8). Now, in the midst of their fall, no king can save them. Some understand that the king given in anger refers to Saul; others think it refers to the kings of the northern kingdom in general. The text does not specify.

For today: before asking God for what we desire so insistently, let us ask ourselves whether we trust in Him or in something that gives us security. Let us seek His will, because only in Him is our true help.
exp.0:2:
Hosea obeys what God commanded him: he marries Gomer, the daughter of Diblaim, she becomes pregnant, and she gives birth to a son. The verse now says "married" and "bore," so we will describe the events in those plain terms: Hosea goes and marries Gomer, and she conceives and bears him a son.

God had asked Hosea to take a woman who would be unfaithful, and his family would serve as a sign to Israel, which was turning away from God to follow other gods.
