Scholars discuss whether Gomer was already unfaithful or would become so later, and whether everything happened literally or as a vision. The text does not make this clear. What is clear is that Hosea obeyed.

God sometimes asks us to obey even when we do not understand the whole plan. We can trust that He is faithful and has a purpose. Today, ask yourself: what simple step of obedience has God shown me that I have been putting off? Take it today with confidence.
exp.11:4:
The passage says that Jacob wrestled with an angel and came out on top, but that he did it weeping and pleading. "Prevailed" means that he achieved what he was seeking. The verse says he wept and sought God's favor. It adds that God found him at Bethel, and that there God spoke with us, that is, with the people descended from Jacob.

Hosea, a prophet of the northern kingdom (Israel), speaks in God's name. God has a legal dispute with Judah and with Israel because of their unfaithfulness. Hosea recalls the story of Jacob, who wrestled with God (Genesis 32) and found God at Bethel (Genesis 28 and 35). Some understand Jacob's strength to be his persistence in prayer; others see in it a warning against trusting one's own strength.

God is not impressed by strength, but by a humble heart that weeps and seeks. Today you can draw near to Him with sincerity, without pretending, and ask Him with confidence. The LORD God of Hosts, the LORD is His name of renown.
exp.9:13:
God says he is about to bring a severe judgment on Israel. There will be a roar of battle rising among its people, and all its fortified cities will be torn down. He compares this to what Shalman did to Beth-arbel in the day of battle, a destruction so brutal that mothers were dashed to pieces along with their children. The phrase "roar of battle" refers to the noise and chaos of war, and "fortresses" are the walled cities that were meant to keep the people safe.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had trusted in its army and in its own way, and not in the Lord. It had sown wickedness and would now reap deception. Who Shalman was and where Beth-arbel stood is uncertain; scholars have interpreted this in several ways.

For today: do not put your security in your strength, your money, or your plans. Seek the Lord with humility, sow justice and mercy, and trust in him.
exp.4:3:
This verse says that the people of Israel no longer have the will to return to God. Their deeds have them trapped. The verse speaks of what their actions have done to them. The phrase "a spirit of prostitution is within them" points to an inner inclination toward spiritual unfaithfulness, that is, worshiping other gods the way a person betrays a spouse. "They do not know the LORD" does not mean they are ignorant of his name, but that they have no real relationship with him. "Return" means to repent.

Context: The prophet Hosea speaks on God's behalf in the eighth century B.C. Ephraim is another name for the northern kingdom, Israel. God accuses them of idolatry and warns that their hearts have grown hard. Hosea often uses the image of a broken marriage to show God's pain.

For today: When something takes the place of God in the heart, it gradually becomes harder to return. Today you can ask yourself what distracts you from him, and take a small step back toward him with a sincere prayer.
exp.10:10:
They will come back trembling, like birds flying from Egypt and like doves returning from the land of Assyria. The word "trembling" describes them coming back in fear or agitation, and "I will settle them" means God will place them back in their homes. God promises to bring them home.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel, also called Ephraim, had turned away from God and faced judgment, with exile and foreign rule. Even so, in this chapter God says he will not destroy his people completely, because he is God and not a man. Scholars debate whether the promise refers only to the return from exile or also to something broader and future.

Today it reminds us that God disciplines, but does not abandon. If you have wandered away, you can return to him with confidence, because his desire is to restore you and give you a home.
exp.8:16:
He says God will reject them, that is, set them aside, because they have not obeyed him. The sense of "reject" here is to cast away or throw out. "Obey" in this verse means to follow in action, not merely to hear. As a result, they will wander without direction, from one place to another, among the nations (the word for nations here refers to foreign peoples).

The prophet Hosea speaks, acting as God's messenger, announcing judgment on Israel, also called Ephraim. Gilgal was a place where the people had fallen into deep wickedness. God charges that, despite his warnings, they went on their own way. Many understand this to announce the exile under Assyria, although the text gives no further detail.

For today: hearing God is more than listening to a message; it is obeying him. Today you can choose one thing God has shown you in his Word and put it into practice with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.4:2:
God knows Ephraim completely, since Ephraim was the leading tribe of the northern kingdom, and so the verse speaks of all of Israel through it. Nothing about Israel is hidden from him. The phrase "turned to prostitution" speaks of spiritual unfaithfulness: leaving God to follow other gods. "Defiled" means stained, made unclean.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Earlier, God had accused the priests and the king of having been a snare and a net, that is, of having trapped the people and led them astray, in places like Mizpah and Tabor. God does not overlook what is happening; that is why judgment is coming, and the people no longer think of returning to him.

For today: God sees even what we try to hide. That is frightening, but it also invites us to return to him with sincerity, without excuses or appearances, trusting that the one who knows us can also forgive us.
exp.3:5:
My people are destroyed because they lack knowledge. Here "knowledge" means knowing God and his law. The priests turned it away on purpose. That is why God says he will reject them from serving as his priests, and since they forgot his law, he will also forget their children.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to Israel, the northern kingdom. He especially accuses the priests, who were supposed to teach the law to the people and did not. Because of that neglect, everyone went astray. Some scholars think the words "I will reject you" refer to the priests, and others think they refer to the whole people.

For today: do not neglect to know God's Word. Set aside time regularly to read it, and if you teach others, do so faithfully, because a lack of knowledge also affects the family.
exp.3:0:
God calls his people to listen. The word rendered "case" here means that God brings them into something like a legal dispute, as in a lawsuit, to present his charge against them. The accusation is that there is no truth in the land (faithfulness and honesty), no loving devotion (steadfast love and compassion), and no knowledge of God (knowing him and living according to his will).

Hosea was a prophet who spoke in the northern kingdom, Israel, in a time of great injustice. God speaks through him. The verses that follow list sins such as lying, stealing, adultery and violence, and warn that the whole land would suffer for them. God does not accuse out of whim; he wants to bring his people back to himself.

For today: consider whether there is truth and compassion in your home and work. Knowing God is not only knowing facts, but reflecting his character in how you speak and treat others.
exp.4:0:
God calls the priests, the house of Israel, and the royal house to pay close attention, because his judgment is coming against them. He tells them, "Hear this," meaning "listen to this," and "Give ear," meaning "pay attention." He accuses them of having been a snare, a trap, at Mizpah, and a net spread out on Tabor. Instead of guiding the people, their leaders led them into a fall.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom of Israel. He accuses the religious and political leaders of leading the people into idolatry. Mizpah and Tabor were well-known places, but it is not known with certainty what practices took place there; some think of false worship or deception.

For today: those who have influence, in the church, the family, or the workplace, carry a greater responsibility. Let us ask God that our example helps others draw near to him, not stumble.
exp.3:16:
This verse says that Ephraim, which is another name for the northern kingdom of Israel, has joined itself completely to idols. That is why God says "leave him alone," meaning "do not keep pressing him, leave him as he is." "Joined to" means devoted or attached to something.

Here God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He has just warned Judah not to imitate the unfaithfulness of Israel. Israel has been stubborn, like a rebellious cow that will not be led. There are different views on the tone of "leave him alone": some see it as a severe judgment, others as a painful warning that lets him suffer the consequences of his own choice.

For today: examine what things are taking the place of God in your heart. If you have hardened your heart, do not wait any longer. Return to Him today, while you can still hear His voice.
exp.8:8:
Israel had sunk very deep into wickedness and had become thoroughly corrupted. The prophet compares this to the days of Gibeah, a reminder of a terrible episode. Saying that God "will remember their guilt" means that he does not overlook what they have done, and "will punish their sins" means that he will come to hold them accountable and deal with their wrongdoing.

The prophet Hosea speaks here, sent by God to the northern kingdom (Ephraim). Gibeah is mentioned in Judges 19, where a dreadful crime took place. Many understand Hosea to show that the people had fallen back into violence and degradation of a similar kind. Interpreters differ on the exact details of the comparison, but the general sense is clear: the sin was deep, and God would respond.

Today we can remember that sin grows when we tolerate it. Let us not wait until we have sunk further; let us confess it soon and return to God, who forgives the one who repents.
exp.4:6:
This verse says that the people were unfaithful to the LORD. "Have been unfaithful" means betraying or breaking a commitment. "Illegitimate children" may refer to children born from a life far from God, or children born from marriages with foreigners or from idolatrous practices; it is understood in several ways. "The New Moon will devour them along with their land" perhaps speaks of a brief time: ruin will come soon and will carry off them and their land.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, who addresses the northern kingdom (Israel or Ephraim) and also warns Judah. They worshiped idols and yet presented offerings, but God had turned away from them. The warning seeks to make them aware of their sin.

Today: it is not enough to offer things to God if the heart is far from Him. Examine your life with sincerity, leave behind what separates you from God, and return to Him with humility, before sin causes you more harm.

sum.11: God accuses Ephraim and Israel of lying and deceiving, of making alliances with other nations and of gaining wealth dishonestly, all while claiming they have done nothing wrong. He reminds them of Jacob, who wrestled and sought God, and calls them to return to Him, to practice mercy and justice, and to always wait on Him. If they do not, they will receive the payment for their deeds.
sum.5: Hosea 6 begins with a call to return to the LORD, who wounds but also heals. But God answers that his people's love is as fleeting as the morning dew. He says he desires mercy and the knowledge of God more than sacrifices, and he denounces Israel and Judah for breaking the covenant, for violence, and for immorality.
sum.1: In Hosea 2, God compares Israel to an unfaithful wife who runs after other lovers (Baal) and forgets that God was the one giving her everything. Because of this, God announces punishment and scarcity, but then promises to lead her into the wilderness, speak tenderly to her heart, and restore her. In the end, God betroths her forever, in righteousness and mercy, and says, "You are my people."
sum.4: God accuses the priests, the king, and the people of Israel of idolatry and pride, and announces punishment for Judah as well. Even if they seek him with sacrifices, they will not find him, because their hearts have turned away and they do not know him. God will act like a moth and like a lion until they recognize their sin and seek him in distress.
sum.0: God tells Hosea to marry Gomer, and their children are given names that announce judgment: Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah ("not pitied"), and Lo-ammi ("not my people"), because Israel has turned away from God. But God promises mercy to Judah and, in the end, to restore his people, calling them "children of the living God."
sum.7: God warns that an enemy will come against Israel because they broke their covenant, set up kings without consulting him, made idols such as the calf of Samaria, and sought alliances with Assyria instead of trusting in him. They sowed the wind and will reap the whirlwind. God rejects their empty sacrifices and announces punishment.
sum.12: God accuses Ephraim (Israel) of forgetting him after receiving prosperity, and of falling into the worship of Baal and the golden calves. Because of this, their reputation will vanish like morning mist, and judgment and destruction will come upon Samaria. Even so, God promises to redeem them from death and the grave, and reminds them that he alone is Savior.
sum.13: The prophet Hosea calls Israel to return to God and ask for forgiveness with sincere words, giving up trust in Assyria, in war horses, and in idols. God promises to heal their rebellion, love them freely, and make them flourish like a lily, an olive tree, and a grapevine. The chapter ends by saying that God's ways are straight: the righteous walk in them, but rebels stumble.
sum.10: God remembers how he loved Israel from the time they were young. He brought them out of Egypt and cared for them tenderly, but the people turned away to other gods and refused to come back to him. Because of this, judgment will come. Yet God's heart is moved, and he decides not to destroy them completely. He promises to bring his children back to their homes.
sum.6: In Hosea 7, God wants to heal Israel, but he uncovers their deceit, their wickedness, and the corruption of their kings and leaders. The people do not cry out to God from the heart; instead, they look for help to Egypt and Assyria, and because of this they will face judgment. God reminds them that he redeemed them and strengthened them, but they rebelled against him.
sum.8: God tells Israel not to rejoice, because it has abandoned him and loved the rewards of idolatry. For this reason it will lose its harvests, be carried off to Egypt and Assyria, and its children will not prosper. The prophets warn, but the people reject them, and God casts them off for not listening to him.
sum.9: Israel, like a lush vine, used its abundance to multiply its altars and idols, and so God will bring judgment: its king will be cut off, the idols will be destroyed, and the people will be taken away to Assyria. But God calls them to sow righteousness and seek Him, because they trusted in their own strength and reaped wickedness.
sum.2: God tells Hosea to love a woman again, even though she has been unfaithful to him, just as God loves Israel even though Israel has turned to other gods. Hosea buys her back and asks her to remain faithful to him for many days. In the same way, Israel will go a long time without a king or worship, but in the end it will return to seek the LORD and his goodness.
sum.3: God accuses Israel because there is no longer any truth, mercy, or knowledge of Him in the land, and lying, theft, adultery, and violence are everywhere. The priests and the people have turned away from the law, sought out idols and vices, and for this reason shame and judgment will come. Judah is warned not to follow that same path.
